ai_guide_link: AI assistance is available for this feature. See the [AI assistant guide](../ai/) for details.
ai_intro: MonaBase is AI-native across five workflows: stored-program and trigger coding, trace-based debugging, SQL creation, SQL tuning and test-data generation. Each assistant starts in the relevant screen with its own context. Choose an OpenAI-compatible provider and model; review what is sent and what is proposed.
ai_note: Requests send selected content to your configured provider and can incur fees. Avoid credentials, confidential data and unnecessary source. AI output can be incorrect; it is not a substitute for testing.
ai_step_1: Configure a compatible Chat Completions endpoint, model and API key in AI settings. Hosted and local providers are supported when they expose the required OpenAI-compatible API; adjust response and timeout limits for your service.
ai_step_2: Start the assistant from the code, trace, SQL, tuning or data-generation screen. Select the required context, state your question, and preview the outgoing request. The provider does not connect directly to your database.
ai_step_3: Review answers, evidence and proposed changes. Apply source edits, execute SQL or insert data only after checking them; compare actual results with the proposal. An adopted summary can be edited for a Git commit.
ai_summary: Five integrated assistants, your choice of provider, no direct AI database access.
check_constraints_create_1_2: Confirm the disabled schema and table fields at the top of the form.
check_constraints_create_1_3: The originating table is fixed. To target another table, open its Structure tab rather than trying to redirect this form.
check_constraints_create_2_2: Enter an explicit name. Oracle input is uppercased; PostgreSQL retains the typed case.
check_constraints_create_2_3: Becomes the name in ADD CONSTRAINT. This form requires a name even though some database SQL supports automatic naming.
check_constraints_create_3_2: Enter only the condition, such as AMOUNT >= 0 AND STATUS IN ('A', 'B'). Do not enter a surrounding CHECK(...) or a full ALTER TABLE command.
check_constraints_create_3_3: The app wraps the expression in CHECK (...). The database validates syntax, permitted expressions and existing data when creation is executed.
check_constraints_create_4_2: Use line numbers and completion for table columns, database objects and DB-specific functions.
check_constraints_create_4_3: Helps compose the condition. A completion suggestion is not proof that a function is legal inside this database’s CHECK expression.
check_constraints_create_5_2: Keep Enable checked to create an active rule, or clear it to create a disabled rule.
check_constraints_create_5_3: Adds ENABLE or DISABLE to Oracle DDL. A disabled rule is defined but not enforced; this control is not available in the PostgreSQL form.
check_constraints_create_6_2: Review the fixed target, required name, expression and any Oracle state setting, then click Create.
check_constraints_create_6_3: Executes ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT CHECK on the main DB connection. Success refreshes the table/sidebar and changes the new form to the created object.
check_constraints_create_7_2: Supply both name and expression; if the DB rejects the statement, read the error before retrying.
check_constraints_create_7_3: Blank required values stop creation before SQL execution. An incompatible rule does not automatically repair existing rows or transform their values.
check_constraints_create_description: From a table’s Structure tab, use Add in the check-constraint list, or double-click an existing constraint to edit it. New constraints show a form; existing constraints have Edit and Source tabs.
check_constraints_create_heading: Edit / create form — define a new rule
check_constraints_edit_1_2: Edit the name, review the ALTER preview below the form and click Change.
check_constraints_edit_1_3: Executes ALTER TABLE RENAME CONSTRAINT. The condition itself remains unchanged; use a nonempty name even in existing-constraint mode.
check_constraints_edit_2_2: Toggle Enable and click Change after reviewing the statement.
check_constraints_edit_2_3: Issues ENABLE/DISABLE CONSTRAINT. Enabling can fail if existing data violates the condition; disabling does not remove or fix records.
check_constraints_edit_3_2: Use the rename control; there is no Enable checkbox in this form.
check_constraints_edit_3_3: This screen does not offer CHECK enable/disable, NOT VALID or VALIDATE controls. Use a separately reviewed SQL workflow for features outside this form.
check_constraints_edit_4_2: Read the stored expression but do not expect direct editing in existing mode.
check_constraints_edit_4_3: Changing the rule needs a deliberately planned replacement. The app does not silently drop and recreate it when only the name or state changes.
check_constraints_edit_5_2: Read the planned ALTER TABLE statement(s) and use the copy icon if needed.
check_constraints_edit_5_3: Updates the read-only preview as name/state inputs change. Oracle may generate state change then rename as separate statements; copying executes neither.
check_constraints_edit_6_2: Click Change only after reviewing the intended operations; if nothing supported differs, read the no-changes message.
check_constraints_edit_6_3: Executes supported statements in order and stops after an error. Earlier successful Oracle DDL may remain effective if a later statement fails; no-changes does not recreate the rule.
check_constraints_edit_7_2: Click Delete and confirm the displayed constraint target.
check_constraints_edit_7_3: Runs ALTER TABLE DROP CONSTRAINT and closes the tab on success. It removes the rule, not existing table rows; later writes are no longer protected by that rule.
check_constraints_edit_description: The existing expression is read-only. Oracle supports rename and enable/disable here; PostgreSQL supports rename only. These operations alter the table’s actual constraint, not a private UI setting.

check_constraints_examples_1_3: The condition is true and the CHECK permits the value; other constraints may still reject the record.
check_constraints_examples_2_3: Zero is allowed. Use a strictly positive expression if zero is not valid for the business rule.
check_constraints_examples_3_3: The condition is false and an enforced CHECK rejects the write; the app does not round or repair the value.
check_constraints_examples_4_3: Evaluates as unknown and does not by itself violate CHECK. It can still be rejected by a separate NOT NULL constraint.
check_constraints_examples_5_2: Condition: AMOUNT IS NOT NULL AND AMOUNT >= 0.

check_constraints_examples_description: Example column: numeric AMOUNT. CHECK normally accepts true or unknown (from NULL), so a nonnegative rule alone does not make the column required. Combine an explicit NULL check or a suitable NOT NULL definition when required.
check_constraints_intro: CHECK constraints validate row conditions inside the database. Existing constraints have Edit and Source tabs; new constraints open a creation form. Edit changes the permitted name/state settings, while Source shows generated ADD DDL. Review these operations separately from the condition itself and the actual database validation state.
check_constraints_note: Constraint changes are DDL. Consider locks, validation time and the effect on pending work before executing.
check_constraints_references_body: For the three-valued result of CHECK expressions and its distinction from NOT NULL, see [Oracle constraint documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/21/sqlrf/constraint.html) and [PostgreSQL 16 constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-CHECK-CONSTRAINTS). The available controls described above refer to MonaBase, not every feature supported by those databases.
check_constraints_replacement_body: Existing expressions are locked, so changing the rule requires a separately planned replacement. Inspect existing rows and the exact definition first; the form provides no automatic backup, migration or refresh/retry button. If the definition looks incomplete or another tool changed it, reopen the window and verify the table’s Structure tab before execution. Oracle ENABLE/ADD and other DDL may validate existing rows, acquire locks and implicitly commit prior work. PostgreSQL controls outside simple add/rename/drop belong in a reviewed SQL workflow.

check_constraints_workflow_body: Open the table’s Structure tab, choose Add in the check-constraint list and enter a name such as CK_ORDER_AMOUNT. Test representative writes only in a dedicated test environment, then inspect the DB result rather than assuming that opening the source tab applied the rule.

connection_intro: Connection profiles keep the database identity, connection color, and transport settings together. Use a name and color that make development and production easy to distinguish. A reachable server still needs a valid account and database privileges.
connection_note: For production inspection, choose read-only mode and a least-privilege account. Read-only mode blocks writes and program/trace execution; it does not replace database permissions. Saved secrets use OS-backed secure storage when available; otherwise new credentials may remain session-only.
connection_oracle: Oracle connections use the configured service. OS authentication requires a supported 64-bit Oracle Client and its folder in Settings. Oracle and PostgreSQL transport options are not interchangeable.
connection_postgresql: TLS with certificate verification requires a TLS-capable server and a trusted certificate matching its hostname. It does not silently fall back to an unencrypted connection when verification fails.
connection_step_1: Choose Oracle or PostgreSQL, enter the host, port, database/service, username and password, then name the profile.
connection_step_2: For inspection tasks, select read-only mode. Choose the available encryption settings; for SSH, enter the jump host and verify its fingerprint against a trusted source on first connection.
connection_step_3: Connect and select the working schema. If authentication fails, check the account and target database rather than repeatedly changing unrelated settings.
connection_summary: Connect directly or through an SSH tunnel.
contact_discussions_body: Use [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/eijiikemura/monabase/discussions) for how-to questions, ideas, feature requests, and community discussion. Discussions are public and require a GitHub account to post.
contact_discussions_heading: 2. Questions and feature requests — GitHub Discussions
contact_intro: MonaBase is an independently developed open-source project. Please choose one of the four channels below according to your inquiry. Public posts can be viewed by anyone. No email or web-form support desk is provided.
contact_issues_body: Use [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/eijiikemura/monabase/issues) for application errors, crashes, incorrect results, or UI problems. Search existing issues before opening a new one. Share reproducible steps and non-sensitive diagnostic details. Issues are public.
contact_privacy_body: GitHub Issues and Discussions are public; private vulnerability reports are restricted to authorized participants; X DMs are not public posts but are processed by X. Using these channels may reveal your account name, message content, and any attachments to the relevant platform and recipients. Each service applies its own privacy policy. Do not provide passwords, API keys, connection strings, confidential database data, private keys, or personal data. Also see the [Privacy Policy](../privacy-policy/).
contact_report_body: Include the MonaBase version; Windows/macOS version; Oracle/PostgreSQL type and version; the affected screen; steps to reproduce; expected and actual behavior; and a sanitized error message or screenshot where useful. Replace hostnames, account names, SQL literals, database records, access tokens and other sensitive values with placeholders before posting.
contact_report_heading: What to include in a bug report
contact_security_body: Do not post suspected vulnerabilities, authentication bypasses, or credential-exposure issues in public Issues. Open [MonaBase Security](https://github.com/eijiikemura/monabase/security) and select **Report a vulnerability** to submit a private security report on GitHub. This channel is for security vulnerabilities only, not general private inquiries. A GitHub account is required. Do not include passwords, API keys, real database records, or other unnecessary sensitive data.
contact_summary: Report bugs, ask questions, suggest features, or contact the developer privately through the appropriate channel.
contact_support_body: MonaBase is maintained by an individual developer. Responses, investigation, fixes and individual support are not guaranteed; times may vary. Support by email and private web form is not provided. Please keep one issue per bug and avoid posting confidential information in public channels.
contact_x_body: For general inquiries that should not be public (excluding vulnerability reports), send a direct message (DM) to [@eijiikemura on X](https://x.com/eijiikemura). **Message requests are accepted from all accounts, regardless of whether they follow the maintainer.** To reduce spam, requests are screened using X’s filters and reviewed before any response. A reply is not guaranteed. An X account is required; no alternative private channel for general inquiries is provided to users without one. Do not send passwords, API keys, database credentials, personal data, or other confidential information. X’s privacy policy applies.
contact_x_heading: 4. Other private inquiries — X direct messages
cross_tab_aggregates_description: The value column is separate from the row/column dimensions. Prefer numeric source values for arithmetic aggregates. PostgreSQL converts non-COUNT values to NUMERIC; Oracle aggregates the selected column with its database type rules.
cross_tab_avg_effect: Calculates the mean for each intersection, excluding NULL values rather than treating them as zero. The current display shows integer portions, so check fractional values separately.
cross_tab_avg_how: Choose AVG on a suitable numeric measure.
cross_tab_axes_description: The same conversion/grouping controls are available on both axes. Changing an axis field resets its grouping choices and selects an initial conversion based on the column type. Date/time columns normally use their native type.
cross_tab_axes_title: Row and column axes: conversion and grouping
cross_tab_cast_effect: Number enables numeric grouping; Date parses values and enables date grouping. String mode groups raw values without those options. Conversions are query expressions, not changes to the stored column type; incompatible values may fail during execution.
cross_tab_cast_how: For eligible non-date columns, choose String, Number or Date. Native date/time columns use None (date type).
cross_tab_class_enable_effect: Groups values into numeric bands rather than one category for every value. This is particularly useful for integer ages, scores or quantities.
cross_tab_class_enable_how: On a Number axis, enable Group by classes.
cross_tab_class_range_effect: Values below the start use a <start category; values above the end use >end. The last band’s label can extend beyond the end, but values greater than the end still go into >end.
cross_tab_class_range_how: Set the main range, for example start 0 and end 99. Keep the end at or above the start.
cross_tab_class_unit_effect: A larger unit creates broader, fewer categories. A unit of zero or less does not activate numeric banding; use positive units and inspect boundary values.
cross_tab_class_unit_how: Enter a positive interval, for example 10 for integer bands 0–9, 10–19 and so on.
cross_tab_column_effect: Distinct non-NULL grouped values become result columns and chart series. There is a maximum of 200 categories; use grouping or filters if there are more.
cross_tab_column_how: Choose the dimension to spread across columns, such as status or month.
cross_tab_copy_effect: Copies the chart as a PNG image with a white background to the clipboard. It is not an editable spreadsheet or a saved chart-settings file; clipboard access must be available.
cross_tab_copy_how: With a chart displayed, click Copy image and paste into a document or chat that accepts images.
cross_tab_count_effect: Oracle counts non-NULL values of the selected measure. The current PostgreSQL implementation counts matching source rows, including rows where that measure is NULL. Use a non-NULL measure to make the distinction irrelevant, or verify with SQL.
cross_tab_date_format_effect: Controls how text is parsed into dates before grouping. It is different from the app’s date display format and the filter date-input format.
cross_tab_date_format_how: Match the source text, for example YYYYMMDD for 20261030 or YYYYMM for 202610.
cross_tab_date_group_effect: Merges values into labels such as 2026, 2026-Q4, 2026-10 or 2026-10-30. With None, time components may produce separate categories; grouping by month retains the year.
cross_tab_date_group_how: Choose None, Year, Quarter, Month or Day on a native/converted date axis.
cross_tab_example_body: Assume the source contains REGION, ORDER_DATE, AMOUNT and STATUS. Choose REGION as Rows, ORDER_DATE as Columns, leave a native date column unconverted and set its grouping to Month. Choose AMOUNT and SUM, then optionally filter STATUS = PAID. Execute to see regions down the rows and year-months across the columns. Switching SUM to AVG changes each cell to an average; switching the date group from Month to Year merges the monthly columns into yearly columns after re-execution.
cross_tab_execute_effect: Reads column categories and aggregates the current database data, then opens Aggregation results. Axis/filter/aggregate changes need another execution to refresh the result and chart.
cross_tab_execute_how: Choose row, column and value fields, then click Execute Cross Tab. The Execute button on Filter conditions runs the same analysis.
cross_tab_export_effect: Exports the held pivot result, not source detail rows or an image. Display formatting and exported values need not look identical, so check fractional values where precision matters.
cross_tab_export_how: Use the result footer’s download action and choose clipboard, CSV or Excel.
cross_tab_filter_clear_effect: Removes filter inputs. It does not automatically rebuild the result or reset the chosen row/column/value configuration.
cross_tab_filter_clear_how: Use the condition panel’s clear button.
cross_tab_filter_execute_effect: Runs the same pivot analysis using the selected axes, aggregation and new filters. These are pre-aggregation conditions, not HAVING conditions on totals.
cross_tab_filter_execute_how: After changing conditions, click Execute on this tab.
cross_tab_filter_search_effect: Only filters the condition controls shown on screen. Conditions hidden by the search still apply to the aggregation.
cross_tab_filter_search_how: Search the column name or enable the active-conditions-only checkbox.
cross_tab_filter_type_effect: Changes how the entered value becomes a SQL condition. This is separate from the axis conversion setting.
cross_tab_filter_type_how: Use String, Number or Date to match the column/value being compared.
cross_tab_filter_value_effect: Do not surround a string input with SQL quotes. Blank values mean no condition, not IS NULL. Invalid numeric input is not a valid numeric filter; verify the entered value before execution.
cross_tab_filter_value_how: Enter PAID for a string comparison or 200 for a numeric comparison; dates follow the app’s date-input format.
cross_tab_filters_description: Filters apply to source rows before categories and aggregates are calculated. Conditions on different columns are combined with AND. This panel does not provide a sort-setting row.
cross_tab_graph_effect: Changes presentation only. Row labels form the horizontal axis, column categories become series, and aggregated measures form the vertical values. Use bar charts for category comparison and interpret lines/areas according to the category order.
cross_tab_graph_how: Open Chart and choose Bar, Line or Area.
cross_tab_group_example_body: For text such as 20261030, choose Date conversion with original format YYYYMMDD, then Month to create 2026-10 categories. For integer ages with start 0, end 99 and unit 10, numeric classes produce 0-9, 10-19, …, 90-99, with <0 and >99 outside the range. These class labels are intended for integer-style bands; review fractional boundary values rather than assuming the label describes a continuous interval exactly. Grouping reduces detail, so compare with a finer grouping when investigating a total.
cross_tab_group_example_title: Examples of date and numeric grouping
cross_tab_intro: Summarize one table or view by a row dimension, column dimension and aggregate measure. The tables below explain source selection, conversions, grouping, filters, result output and charts. The database computes the aggregate; changing a setting requires re-execution unless it only changes presentation.
cross_tab_layout_effect: Allocates more space to settings or results without changing the analysis or rerunning the query.
cross_tab_layout_how: Drag the horizontal divider between the configuration and results.
cross_tab_load_effect: Restores source, axes, conversions, grouping, aggregation and filters, and retrieves source columns. Results are cleared; execute again. The referenced object/columns must exist in the current database.
cross_tab_load_how: Open a saved cross-tab JSON file.
cross_tab_log_effect: Provides a record of executed analysis and errors. The shown duration is for the aggregate query, not all setup and category-fetch work.
cross_tab_log_how: Read the generated aggregate SQL and duration in Execution log. If a query fails, inspect the message on this tab.
cross_tab_max_effect: Returns the maximum per intersection. For PostgreSQL, the current query converts the measure to a number, so arbitrary non-numeric text is not suitable.
cross_tab_max_how: Choose MAX to compare maximum values.
cross_tab_min_effect: Returns the minimum per intersection, with the same type-conversion considerations as MAX.
cross_tab_min_how: Choose MIN to compare minimum values.
cross_tab_note: Cross-tab settings and charts summarize the selected source; they do not change its data. The current COUNT behavior differs between Oracle/PostgreSQL for NULL measures, and formatted results show integer portions. Check the detailed notes before relying on exact counts or fractional amounts.
cross_tab_nulls_body: Column categories are discovered from non-NULL column-axis expressions; there is no automatic separate NULL column. COUNT currently differs between databases: Oracle uses COUNT(measure), while PostgreSQL counts matching rows. A NULL measure therefore needs explicit checking. PostgreSQL uses numeric conversion for SUM/AVG/MAX/MIN, so non-numeric text can fail. The column-category limit is 200 after grouping and filters. If no categories remain or the limit is exceeded, review filters, date conversion and grouping. Use a direct aggregate query to verify totals, counts and NULL handling under the same conditions.
cross_tab_number_display_effect: The current cross-tab formatter displays only the integer portion, including chart labels/tooltips. This does not mean the underlying aggregate is an integer or was rounded; inspect SQL or exported values for exact fractional results.
cross_tab_number_display_how: Use Settings → View → Number format for none, comma, period or space grouping. Reopen/reload the analysis if needed.
cross_tab_object_effect: Changes the analysis source and clears the previous setup/results. Click Start setup to load the selected object’s columns.
cross_tab_object_type_effect: Changes which source objects appear in the list and resets the analysis settings/results. It does not convert or create database objects.
cross_tab_object_type_how: Choose TABLE, VIEW or MATERIALIZED VIEW.
cross_tab_operator_effect: Changes equality, inequality, range comparison or pattern matching. For LIKE patterns, enter wildcards explicitly, for example %Tokyo%.
cross_tab_output_description: The result grid and chart share the most recently generated pivot data. Switching chart style or copying/exporting that result does not execute another aggregate query.
cross_tab_results_effect: The first column is the row dimension; later columns are categories. Each cell is the selected aggregate for that intersection. Missing combinations may show NULL/blank or zero depending on the database and aggregate.
cross_tab_results_how: Open Aggregation results after executing; scroll horizontally for additional categories.
cross_tab_reuse_body: Save JSON when you want to repeat the same analysis. Loading restores the configuration and clears the old result; execute to read current database data. Merely changing axis/filter/aggregation controls leaves the previous result until the next execution. Changing the source resets fields, filters and results. Running setup reloads columns, initial axis/measure choices and filters and clears the result. Chart type changes reuse the held result immediately. Cross-tab analysis does not create a database pivot table or update source rows.
cross_tab_reuse_title: Save a reusable setup and rerun it
cross_tab_row_effect: Each distinct grouped value becomes a result row. In the chart, these row labels become the horizontal category axis.
cross_tab_row_how: Choose the dimension to list vertically, such as region, customer or order date.
cross_tab_save_effect: Saves the source and analysis configuration for reuse, not result data or a chart image. Chart type is not included in this settings file. It does not change database definitions.
cross_tab_save_how: Click Save after selecting a source and loading its columns; choose a JSON destination.
cross_tab_schema_effect: Refreshes the object list and resets the selected object, fields, filters and existing pivot results. Set up the new source again.
cross_tab_schema_how: Select the schema containing the source.
cross_tab_setup_effect: Loads column names/types and opens Pivot settings and Filter conditions. Initial row/column/value choices are provided; review them before executing. Setup does not yet generate a pivot result.
cross_tab_setup_how: After selecting an object, click Start setup.
cross_tab_source_description: Choose one table, view or materialized view as the source. To analyze joined or calculated data, prepare a suitable database view first. Selecting a source is separate from executing the aggregation.
cross_tab_source_title: Choose a source and prepare the analysis
cross_tab_step_1: Choose the schema, source type and object, then click Start setup to load its columns.
cross_tab_step_2: Choose row, column and measure fields. Set conversions/grouping, the aggregate method and any source-row filters, then execute.
cross_tab_step_3: Read the result, compare with a direct SQL aggregate and check the database-specific NULL/count and decimal display behavior. View a chart, export results or save the setup as needed.
cross_tab_sum_effect: Totals values within each intersection after filtering. Review NULL/empty combinations and the numeric display note below before comparing exact amounts.
cross_tab_sum_how: Choose SUM to total a numeric measure.
cross_tab_summary: Summarize a table or view with row/column groups and charts.
cross_tab_value_effect: Changes what is totaled or compared at each row/column intersection. Axis type-conversion controls do not convert this measure column.
cross_tab_value_how: Choose amount, quantity or another measure. A selected value column is required even for COUNT.
data_generator_ai_body: Use the AI request action in Data generator. MonaBase prepares column definitions and the current JSON settings template, plus foreign-key context and up to 100 referenced sample values per relationship when retrieval succeeds. Describe the scenario and ask AI to return generation-rule JSON. Review and apply the proposed settings, then preview the rows; the AI service does not connect directly to the database or insert rows. Reference samples included in the request are sent to your configured provider.
data_generator_ai_heading: Ask AI for a realistic scenario
data_generator_boundaries_body: Choice values can supply meaningful fictional names or valid parent IDs; regex can shape codes and postal formats. Generation rules operate per column: they do not automatically guarantee cross-column conditions such as shipment after order date, exact status distributions or uniqueness against existing rows. Check those relationships, database constraints and triggers with a small preview/test run. Use synthetic or approved non-sensitive reference data.
data_generator_intro: Build test data with business-like formats and values tailored to your application. Combine sequences, format patterns, plausible amounts, statuses and date ranges for the selected table. Use AI to propose the generation settings, then review the preview before inserting.
data_generator_note: Generation is a real INSERT workflow. Database constraints and triggers still apply, and partial insertion is possible.
data_generator_options_1_2: For nullable generated columns, enter a percentage from `0` to `100`. Not available for NOT NULL or unspecified/excluded columns.
data_generator_options_1_3: Exercise optional values, missing-data searches and NULL handling. This is a per-row probability, not an exact final count.
data_generator_options_1_4: `20` gives each generated row a 20% chance of NULL.
data_generator_options_2_2: Enable Unique for random number, string or date rules; provide enough distinct values for the requested rows.
data_generator_options_2_3: Avoid duplicates within that generated column for this run. It does not pre-check every existing database value.
data_generator_options_2_4: A range with only ten distinct values cannot supply 100 unique rows.
data_generator_options_3_2: Set a positive row count, configure columns and inspect the preview before inserting. If settings change, create a new preview.
data_generator_options_3_3: Start small, check realistic formats and required fields, then insert a reviewed dataset.
data_generator_options_3_4: Preview an order scenario first, then execute 100 rows after checking the target.
data_generator_options_4_2: Save generation settings as JSON and load them for the matching table.
data_generator_options_4_3: Reuse generation rules across test runs; random output is newly generated rather than reproduced from a fixed seed.
data_generator_options_4_4: Keep a reviewed order-data configuration for repeated regression checks.
data_generator_options_description: Combine the rules with NULL probability, uniqueness, a row count and reusable settings.
data_generator_prompt_body: “Prepare settings for 100 fictional orders. Use sequential IDs starting at 1001, formatted order codes, NEW/PAID/SHIPPED statuses, amounts from 100 to 10000 in 0.01 increments, and dates in January 2026. Use the supplied valid customer IDs as choices. Give the nullable memo column a 20% NULL probability. Keep the existing schema and return the JSON configuration.” Adjust column names and types to your table before sending.
data_generator_recipe_1_3: A simple identifier for each generated order.
data_generator_recipe_2_2: Regex `ORD-[0-9]{6}`; enable Unique if enough distinct codes are available.
data_generator_recipe_3_2: Choice of valid IDs from the parent table, for example `101,102,103` when those rows exist.
data_generator_recipe_3_3: Orders linked to existing test customers.
data_generator_recipe_4_3: Multiple states for filtering and grouping tests.
data_generator_recipe_5_3: Prices with a range and decimal values.
data_generator_recipe_6_2: Random date range within January 2026; include time if the column supports it.
data_generator_recipe_6_3: Orders spread across a reporting period.
data_generator_recipe_6_4: A date/time within the chosen range.
data_generator_recipe_7_3: Readable fictional notes plus optional-field cases.
data_generator_recipe_description: Assume an order table with these compatible columns. Match the rules to your actual schema; the examples are fictional and do not promise exact random output.
data_generator_rules_10_2: Choose Fixed and enter the value appropriate to the column type.
data_generator_rules_10_3: A shared test marker, tenant code or a specific boundary case.
data_generator_rules_10_4: Set a text marker to `DEMO` or a numeric quantity to `0`.
data_generator_rules_11_2: Unspecified omits the column from INSERT and is unavailable for NOT NULL columns in the selector. Unsupported column types are excluded automatically.
data_generator_rules_11_3: Allow database defaults or nullable-column behavior to apply; avoid trying to generate unsupported values.
data_generator_rules_11_4: An omitted defaulted column uses its database default. Existing triggers and constraints still apply.
data_generator_rules_1_2: Choose Sequence; set the start and increment.
data_generator_rules_1_3: Predictable numeric IDs or counters, including decimal increments where the column permits them.
data_generator_rules_2_2: For a text column, set a prefix or enable padding. Zero padding uses the column length; the final value including its prefix must fit.
data_generator_rules_2_3: Readable product/order codes or fixed-width identifiers.
data_generator_rules_2_4: Prefix `ORD-` → `ORD-1`. Separately, padding in a six-character column → `000001`.
data_generator_rules_3_2: Choose Sequential date and enter the starting date. Subsequent rows advance one day at a time.
data_generator_rules_3_3: Daily schedules, calendar rows or ordered date-based scenarios.
data_generator_rules_3_4: Start `2026/01/01` → January 1, 2, 3…; display follows your date format.
data_generator_rules_4_2: Set minimum, maximum and rounding unit; optionally enable Unique. The rounding unit is the interval between generated values.
data_generator_rules_4_3: Prices, quantities, scores and representative numeric ranges.
data_generator_rules_4_4: Min `0`, max `1000`, unit `0.01` → values such as `19.99` and `845.20`.
data_generator_rules_5_2: Choose Random string, then alphabetic, numeric or alphanumeric characters. Padding fills to the supported column length; Unique avoids duplicates within this generation.
data_generator_rules_5_3: Synthetic labels, tokens and string-length boundary data.
data_generator_rules_5_4: Alphanumeric → `A7k29`. Use padding to exercise longer column values.
data_generator_rules_6_2: In the Japanese app interface, select Full-width under Random string.
data_generator_rules_6_3: Synthetic full-width text for Japanese input and length/encoding checks; not automatically realistic personal names.
data_generator_rules_6_4: Check how full-width text is stored, displayed and exported.
data_generator_rules_7_2: Choose Random string → Regular expression and enter a supported pattern. The generated string must fit the target column.
data_generator_rules_7_3: Formatted postal codes, product IDs or other synthetic business identifiers.
data_generator_rules_8_2: Set the date range; enable Include time when needed. Unique is available. Date/time input and supported precision depend on the column type and settings.
data_generator_rules_8_3: Order timestamps, reservation dates and activity within a test period.
data_generator_rules_8_4: Choose January 2026, with time enabled, for order timestamps during that month.
data_generator_rules_9_2: Enter comma-separated candidates. Each generated value is selected from that list; no separate percentage-weight setting is provided.
data_generator_rules_9_3: Status codes, fictional company names or known valid parent IDs.
data_generator_rules_9_4: `NEW,PAID,SHIPPED` or fictional company names. For foreign keys, use IDs that actually exist.
data_generator_rules_description: Choose a rule for each supported column. The following options are shared by Oracle and PostgreSQL, subject to the column type. On narrow screens, scroll the table horizontally.
data_generator_step_1: Use the table selection button. The selector starts with the table category selected and shows the first 100 tables in the current schema.
data_generator_step_2: Configure each column using the rule tables below, or request a JSON configuration from AI and review it. Set the row count and preview formats, required values and valid references.
data_generator_step_3: Choose Execute after reviewing the preview. Inspect confirmed inserted rows and any failure before committing or retrying.
data_generator_summary: Create realistic fictional test data with column rules and AI assistance.
database_links_intro: A database link allows Oracle-side SQL to reach another database. The network path originates from the database server, which may differ from the connection path used by your desktop.
database_links_oracle: CREATE DATABASE LINK and ALTER DATABASE LINK require their respective privileges. Public links require broader privileges than private links.
database_links_step_1: Open a link and inspect its name, scope, remote account and connection descriptor without exposing secrets.
database_links_step_2: Use the connection check where available. Confirm the remote target before executing any remote operation.
database_links_step_3: Review credential updates or removal carefully; refresh afterwards to distinguish success from an unconfirmed outcome.
database_links_summary: Inspect and manage Oracle links to remote databases.
dblink_detail_common_1_2: Click Reload at the top right.
dblink_detail_common_1_3: Fetches the link definition and current permissions. Some unsaved edits may be preserved; review the fields before executing.
dblink_detail_common_2_2: Switch tabs for an existing link.
dblink_detail_common_2_3: Does not modify the database. Source and Information describe the saved link.
dblink_detail_common_3_2: Click Retry on an error alert.
dblink_detail_common_3_3: Reloads the definition. Tests or changes may remain disabled until recovery.
dblink_detail_common_4_2: Open a read-only connection or a link owned by someone else.
dblink_detail_common_4_3: Edits and deletion are restricted. Managing public links requires separate privileges.
dblink_detail_common_description: Existing database links have Edit, Source, and Information tabs. Creation uses a separate form. Controls are unavailable while reloading.
dblink_detail_console_1_2: Inspect timestamps, results, SQL, and error codes.
dblink_detail_console_1_3: Helps determine which operation succeeded or failed.
dblink_detail_console_2_3: Clears the displayed log only; the database link is unchanged.
dblink_detail_console_3_2: Click Close or drag the splitter.
dblink_detail_console_3_3: Changes only the console visibility/width, not the database.
dblink_detail_console_description: The console opens on successful/failed operations. Logged SQL is for review, not automatic execution.
dblink_detail_edit_10_2: Click Delete on an existing link and confirm.
dblink_detail_edit_10_3: Runs DROP DATABASE LINK and closes the tab on success. Check dependent usage first.
dblink_detail_edit_1_2: Select only when creating a link.
dblink_detail_edit_1_3: Creates a public database link visible by name across users. Existing link scope cannot be changed.
dblink_detail_edit_2_2: Shows the current user or PUBLIC.
dblink_detail_edit_2_3: Read-only field; this form does not choose another private owner.
dblink_detail_edit_3_2: Enter a name while creating the link.
dblink_detail_edit_3_3: Converted to uppercase; Oracle domain may be appended to form the full name. Cannot be renamed here.
dblink_detail_edit_4_3: Changing the stored user requires dropping and recreating the existing link.
dblink_detail_edit_5_2: Enter on create or recreate, or to rotate an existing password.
dblink_detail_edit_5_3: Required for creation/recreation. Changing only the password plans ALTER; the field is cleared after success.
dblink_detail_edit_6_2: Enter an Oracle connection identifier or connection string.
dblink_detail_edit_6_3: Changing it plans DROP and CREATE. Resolution is from the Oracle database server side.
dblink_detail_edit_7_2: Review the generated SQL below the form or copy it.
dblink_detail_edit_7_3: Shows CREATE, ALTER, or DROP+CREATE; preview does not execute SQL and masks passwords.
dblink_detail_edit_8_2: Click Test connection for an existing link.
dblink_detail_edit_8_3: Explicitly tests the saved link, not unexecuted form edits; displays elapsed time on success.
dblink_detail_edit_9_2: Fill in the form and click Execute.
dblink_detail_edit_9_3: May require confirmation. Validation, permissions, and changes determine availability; success modifies the DB definition.
dblink_detail_edit_description: These fields create or modify a database link. Name and visibility cannot be changed after creation. The SQL preview masks the password.
dblink_detail_info_1_3: Identifies the link and cannot be edited in this tab.
dblink_detail_info_2_2: Check FIXED, CONNECTED, CURRENT, or other reported modes.
dblink_detail_info_2_3: Displays catalog metadata only. Unsupported authentication types may be read-only.
dblink_detail_info_3_2: Review the USING target and creation timestamp.
dblink_detail_info_3_3: No changes occur. Valid connectivity is not guaranteed without a test.
dblink_detail_info_4_3: Tests the persisted link explicitly and reports success or failure.
dblink_detail_info_description: This tab primarily displays the saved link metadata. Connectivity is tested only on explicit request.
dblink_detail_info_heading: Information tab: stored definition and connectivity
dblink_detail_safety_1_2: Values match the saved definition and password is blank.
dblink_detail_safety_2_2: Fill the password of an existing link only.
dblink_detail_safety_3_2: Change the username or USING target.
dblink_detail_safety_3_3: Requires DROP+CREATE with confirmation. If creation fails after dropping, the link may remain absent.
dblink_detail_safety_4_2: Another operation changed the definition, permissions are missing, or reload fails.
dblink_detail_safety_4_3: Execution may fail or be blocked. Review errors and the console, then reload before retrying.
dblink_detail_safety_5_2: Create or delete a public link.
dblink_detail_safety_5_3: Has wider scope and requires privileges/confirmation. Does not grant remote access rights by itself.
dblink_detail_safety_description: Database links carry credentials and remote targets. Preview is informational; changes and tests require explicit actions.
dblink_detail_source_1_2: View the current definition in Source.
dblink_detail_source_1_3: Read-only reference DDL; viewing or copying does not alter the database.
dblink_detail_source_2_2: Appears when a change is planned.
dblink_detail_source_2_3: Shows the intended ALTER or recreation; updates when form inputs change.
dblink_detail_source_3_2: Click the copy icon for either code panel.
dblink_detail_source_3_3: Copies the corresponding text to the clipboard; failures are reported.
dblink_detail_source_description: Keep the saved-definition template separate from planned changes. The saved template cannot recover the original password.
dblink_detail_source_heading: Source tab: saved template and pending SQL
er_detail_auto_1_2: Select a schema for the diagram
er_detail_auto_1_3: Loads table candidates and relationship metadata for the selected schema.
er_detail_auto_2_3: Targets a selected table or the complete schema when drawing.
er_detail_auto_3_2: Click Draw with the current selection
er_detail_auto_3_3: Retrieves metadata and redraws the diagram without modifying database definitions.
er_detail_auto_4_3: Shows or hides comments for tables and columns.
er_detail_auto_5_3: Toggles use of available comments as the primary displayed names.
er_detail_auto_6_3: Shows or hides column data types in the diagram.
er_detail_auto_7_3: Exports the currently displayed diagram to a PNG image.
er_detail_auto_description: Builds a diagram from existing foreign-key metadata. Display options affect the diagram, not the database.
er_detail_custom_1_3: Starts a new editable custom diagram.
er_detail_custom_2_2: Select an entry or its delete icon
er_detail_custom_2_3: Opens the saved diagram or requests deletion of that saved diagram.
er_detail_custom_4_3: Changes the scope of tables and views available for addition.
er_detail_custom_5_2: Search and choose objects in the add dialog
er_detail_custom_5_3: Adds nodes to the diagram; it does not create database objects.
er_detail_custom_6_3: Changes how names, comments, and types appear in the diagram.
er_detail_custom_7_3: Updates node positions; changes remain unsaved until saved.
er_detail_custom_8_2: Use the Undo or Redo button
er_detail_custom_description: Edits locally saved diagrams with layout and virtual relationships. The schema controls the diagram scope.
er_detail_custom_heading: Custom ER diagram: create and edit
er_detail_history_1_2: Choose the action according to Git availability
er_detail_history_1_3: Saves a local diagram or proceeds to a Git commit when a local repository is available.
er_detail_history_2_2: Enter text in the Git dialog
er_detail_history_2_3: Adds an optional description to identify the saved revision.
er_detail_history_3_3: Reviews database-object changes before applying them to the diagram.
er_detail_history_4_2: Open comparison and select a revision
er_detail_history_4_3: Shows earlier and current diagrams side by side with change indicators.
er_detail_history_5_3: Restores a prior diagram revision, not database definitions.
er_detail_history_6_3: Exports the diagram image or closes the custom editor.
er_detail_history_description: Saving and Git actions affect diagram files and history, not database foreign keys or object definitions.
er_detail_history_heading: Custom ER diagram: save, sync, and history
er_detail_relation_1_3: Opens the dialog for parent/child objects and cardinality.
er_detail_relation_2_3: Changes the endpoints of the diagram relation.
er_detail_relation_3_3: Changes symbols at relationship endpoints; no database constraint is applied.
er_detail_relation_4_3: Applies virtual-relation edits to the diagram.
er_detail_relation_5_3: Edits or removes the selected virtual relation from the diagram.
er_detail_relation_description: Relationship lines are diagram metadata, not actual database foreign-key constraints.
er_diagrams_intro: Custom ER diagrams are first-class Git-managed design artifacts, not just exported images. Save table/view layouts and diagram relationships, record revisions as the design evolves, and retain earlier versions beside your stored source. Diagram edits remain separate from applying database constraints.
er_diagrams_note: A custom diagram is not a schema migration. Review actual database foreign keys in table metadata when you need enforcement guarantees.
er_diagrams_step_1: Open an ER diagram or create a custom one. Use Add table to search tables and views in pages of 100.
er_diagrams_step_2: Arrange objects, inspect keys and columns, and add supported diagram relationships. Check schema names when objects share a name.
er_diagrams_step_3: Save the diagram and record a reviewed revision in Git when needed. Reopen it to continue from the saved layout.
er_diagrams_summary: Explore relationships and version custom diagrams.
getting_started_detail_1_10_1: If Run anyway is unavailable; Store edition
getting_started_detail_1_10_2: If an organization policy prevents running the app, consult your administrator. If a Microsoft Store edition is available, consider installing from the Store instead.
getting_started_detail_1_10_3: Do not disable SmartScreen for the whole device. SmartScreen prompts can differ between Store distribution and unsigned direct downloads.
getting_started_detail_1_1_2: Choose the download for your operating system and CPU from the official GitHub Releases page.
getting_started_detail_1_1_3: Installation steps depend on the package. If no release exists, there is no published distribution to download.
getting_started_detail_1_2_2: Run the Windows x64 installer and follow its prompts.

getting_started_detail_2_2_2: Select a profile in the list.
getting_started_detail_2_2_3: Loads its values into the form; selection alone does not connect.

getting_started_detail_2_3_3: Filters visible profiles only; does not change saved settings or the database.

getting_started_detail_3_4_2: Specify the PostgreSQL database or Oracle service identifier as appropriate.

getting_started_intro: MonaBase is a desktop database IDE for Oracle Database 12+ and PostgreSQL. It connects to a database you provide; it does not include a database server. Git integration and an optional AI assistant extend the same workspace.
getting_started_note: Build provenance can be verified with GitHub Artifact Attestations. This is separate from OS code signing; check release notes for signing status. Never enter production credentials into an unfamiliar build.
getting_started_step_1: Open the project's Releases page and choose the Windows x64 installer, Windows portable EXE, or macOS Apple Silicon DMG. If no release is listed yet, a downloadable version has not been published.
getting_started_step_2: On Windows, install or launch the portable EXE. On Mac, open the DMG and copy MonaBase to Applications. macOS 13 or later is required.
getting_started_step_3: Prepare a database account, connect from the login screen, then open a table or SQL window from the workspace. Configure Git and AI only when you need them.
getting_started_summary: Install MonaBase and make your first database connection.

git_detail_compare_1_3: Loads the two source snapshots and updates the diff; does not restore either revision.
git_detail_compare_2_2: Swap left and right revision selections.
git_detail_compare_2_3: Reverses the comparison direction and added/deleted highlights.
git_detail_compare_3_3: Only changes the visual layout, not repository content.
git_detail_compare_4_2: Move between pages when additional revisions exist.
git_detail_compare_4_3: Loads another page of history for selection.
git_detail_compare_description: Compare any two available recorded revisions for the selected object.
git_detail_current_1_2: Read the displayed database definition in the read-only editor.
git_detail_current_1_3: Does not edit the database or the local Git file.
git_detail_current_2_2: Open the commit dialog for the displayed database object.
git_detail_current_2_3: Requires an initialized repository; opening the dialog does not commit.
git_detail_current_3_2: Enter an optional history description in the dialog.
git_detail_current_3_3: Sets the message for the planned Git commit; the database source remains unchanged.
git_detail_current_4_2: For FUNCTION, PROCEDURE, TRIGGER, PACKAGE, or PACKAGE BODY, use the saved summary of the most recent adopted AI change from the AI conversation history.
git_detail_current_4_3: Fills the Git commit message field with the existing summary without sending a new AI request. Review the message before committing; if no adopted summary is available, the existing message is left unchanged.
git_detail_current_5_3: Records the database-source snapshot in the configured Git workspace; does not run SQL against the DB.
git_detail_current_6_2: Copy displayed SQL, or refresh the current definition from the database.
git_detail_current_6_3: Copy affects the clipboard; refresh updates the comparison source, not the DB definition.
git_detail_current_description: Displays database source and actions for recording it in Git.
git_detail_history_1_2: Click a revision in the version list.
git_detail_history_1_3: Changes the past-source selection and displayed diff; no Git commit is made.
git_detail_history_2_2: Switch the comparison layout using the diff controls.
git_detail_history_2_3: Changes only the way additions and deletions are displayed.
git_detail_history_3_2: Use each pane’s search button or Ctrl/Cmd+F on the focused pane.
git_detail_history_3_3: Highlights matching text; Enter moves to the next hit, without changing the source.
git_detail_history_4_2: Refresh the displayed database source and revision list.
git_detail_history_4_3: Updates the display to newly fetched data; database objects are not modified.
git_detail_history_5_2: Select a past revision, then open its recovery statement.
git_detail_history_5_3: Opens SQL for review; execution or compilation is a separate explicit operation.
git_detail_history_description: Review revisions and open recovery SQL without automatically executing it.
git_detail_remote_1_2: Use the Git menu to confirm pulling from the configured remote.
git_detail_remote_1_3: Fetches/merges remote changes into the workspace; affected object tabs should be reopened to reflect changes.
git_detail_remote_2_2: Open the conflict dialog if Pull reports merge conflicts.
git_detail_remote_2_3: Review conflicted files individually before completing the merge.
git_detail_remote_3_2: Confirm abort when a merge is in progress and should not continue.
git_detail_remote_3_3: Aborts the in-progress Git merge; it does not roll back database SQL changes.
git_detail_remote_4_2: Use the Git remote and local credential configuration supported by the environment.
git_detail_remote_4_3: Authentication/network errors prevent synchronization; never paste tokens into public reports.
git_detail_remote_description: Remote synchronization is distinct from database compilation and local commits.
git_detail_schema_1_2: Choose all or one supported object category, then run Refresh.
git_detail_schema_1_3: Scans the selected schema category and rebuilds the review list; this does not commit.
git_detail_schema_2_3: Filters the displayed rows; it does not discard or overwrite source files.
git_detail_schema_3_2: Select individual objects whose database source differs from recorded Git source.
git_detail_schema_3_3: Controls which reviewed objects will be included in the commit.
git_detail_schema_4_2: Switch comparison between recorded Git source and local working file.
git_detail_schema_4_3: Changes the left-hand baseline; the right side remains current database source.
git_detail_schema_5_2: Enter a message and commit selected changed objects.
git_detail_schema_5_3: Rechecks that DB source has not changed since the scan, then commits; does not update the DB.
git_detail_schema_6_2: Cancel while the schema review is scanning.
git_detail_schema_6_3: Stops using the in-progress scan result; no partial commit occurs.
git_detail_schema_description: Review current database definitions alongside recorded and local sources, then commit selected differences.

git_detail_setup_1_3: Shows local repository status and remote setup; opening does not change Git.

git_detail_setup_4_2: Review the current branch detected from the repository.

git_intro: Version control is for database design as well as code. MonaBase records stored source and custom ER diagrams in Git: review source changes and revisions, keep earlier diagram designs, and prepare recovery SQL in the same workspace.
git_note: Committing, pulling or opening recovery SQL does not apply that SQL to the database. Review and execute database changes separately. Use a dedicated working repository rather than your app source checkout.
git_step_1: Choose a Git working folder and open an object Git tab. Review the source difference before entering a commit message.
git_step_2: Use Schema changes to compare database definitions, recorded Git source and local files. Select related changes and review them before recording a batch.
git_step_3: Compare two revisions or open recovery SQL from history. For a remote repository, review Pull conflicts per file and complete or abort the merge explicitly.
git_summary: Record stored source, compare revisions and review schema changes.
indexes_create_10_2: Review the target, type, options and ordered keys/expression, then click Create after column loading succeeds.
indexes_create_10_3: Executes CREATE INDEX, or PostgreSQL primary-key DDL, on the main DB connection. The sidebar and window identity update after success; this is not a dry run.
indexes_create_1_2: Select the target schema when creating an index.
indexes_create_1_3: Changes the table search scope and clears the selected table/columns so they cannot remain attached to the previous schema. Existing-index schema is fixed.
indexes_create_2_2: Enter the index name; in existing-index mode, change it only when renaming is intended. Oracle input is uppercased by the form.
indexes_create_2_3: Names the new index or prepares an ALTER INDEX rename. Changing text alone does not change the DB.
indexes_create_3_2: Click the table button, search within the selected schema and choose one table from the 100-item pages.
indexes_create_3_3: Loads that table’s available columns. Switching tables clears previous key selections; only tables, not views, are offered.
indexes_create_4_2: Oracle: table index or function-based index. PostgreSQL: table index, primary key or expression index.
indexes_create_4_3: Switches between column selection and an expression editor. PostgreSQL primary-key mode creates an ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT PRIMARY KEY statement, not just a standalone index.
indexes_create_5_2: Enable UNIQUE during creation; PostgreSQL primary-key mode enables it automatically and locks the checkbox.
indexes_create_5_3: Creates a uniqueness-enforcing definition. Existing duplicates can cause creation to fail; NULL behavior follows the database’s rules. Existing uniqueness is read-only here.
indexes_create_6_2: Select available columns on the left and use →, or double-click a column. Use ← or double-click on the right to remove it.
indexes_create_6_3: Builds the index key list. Removing a key from the draft does not drop a column from the table.
indexes_create_7_2: Use Ctrl on Windows/Linux or Command on macOS for individual selections, Shift for ranges, or drag across the list.
indexes_create_7_3: Moves multiple selected columns together. Selection itself does not execute any SQL.
indexes_create_8_2: Select one target column on the right, then use the up/down buttons or Alt+Up/Down.
indexes_create_8_3: Changes the key order in generated DDL. Composite key order affects how queries can use the index; it is not a sort instruction for displayed table rows.
indexes_create_9_2: Choose function/expression mode and enter an expression such as LOWER("EMAIL"). Use completion for functions and table columns.
indexes_create_9_3: Uses the expression as the index key. The app checks for empty text and mismatched parentheses; allowed functions and expression validity are still checked by the DB.
indexes_create_description: Existing indexes open with Edit, Statistics and Source tabs. New indexes show a creation form without those tabs. Target/type/key controls are editable during creation; most become read-only for an existing index.
indexes_create_heading: Edit / create form — choose the target and keys
indexes_delete_1_2: Read the constraint name/kind, owning table and reference count shown above the form.
indexes_delete_1_3: Explains which integrity rule relies on the index. Multiple constraints or foreign-key references can block deletion.
indexes_delete_2_2: Click Delete and confirm the exact schema/index target.
indexes_delete_2_3: Executes DROP INDEX when no protected constraint owns it. Table records are not deleted, but access paths and query performance can change.
indexes_delete_3_2: Inspect the associated primary-key or unique constraint in the table structure workflow.
indexes_delete_3_3: Direct index deletion is blocked. The app does not silently drop the constraint or add CASCADE to bypass it.
indexes_delete_4_2: Read the stronger constraint-removal confirmation when the index belongs to a single constraint without foreign-key references.
indexes_delete_4_3: Uses ALTER TABLE DROP CONSTRAINT rather than DROP INDEX, removing its integrity rule too. Foreign-key references or multiple owning constraints block the operation.
indexes_delete_5_2: If a changed-definition or load error appears, reload/retry and review the target again.
indexes_delete_5_3: Fetches fresh definition/dependencies before planning deletion and refuses a changed target. This protection does not eliminate concurrent changes or replace DB privilege checks.
indexes_delete_description: An index may enforce a primary key or unique/exclusion constraint. Review the constraint notice and foreign-key reference count before deleting; removing an ordinary index and removing a constraint are different operations.
indexes_delete_heading: Edit tab — deletion and constraint protection
indexes_edit_1_2: Edit the name, review the ALTER statement and click Change.
indexes_edit_1_3: Renames the existing index. It does not change its keys, uniqueness, expression or original access method.
indexes_edit_2_3: Shows existing structure without replacing it. A key/type change needs a separately reviewed recreation or migration plan, preserving constraints and dependencies.
indexes_edit_3_2: Read the generated ALTER SQL below the form, and use its copy icon if needed.
indexes_edit_3_3: Updates the planned SQL as editable settings change. Preview is read-only; copying does not run it, and the Source tab still shows the fetched existing definition.
indexes_edit_4_2: Read the unchanged hint if no supported field differs.
indexes_edit_4_3: Does not rebuild or recreate the index just because Change is pressed. Use the appropriate separate SQL workflow if maintenance is intended.
indexes_edit_5_2: Use Retry after an index or column metadata read fails.
indexes_edit_5_3: Retains previously loaded content but blocks execution/deletion until the target metadata loads successfully. A missing definition is not treated as a new empty index.
indexes_edit_6_2: Read SQL, result and errors in the console. Drag its boundary, close it with × or clear displayed logs with the trash icon.
indexes_edit_6_3: Changes presentation only. If several Oracle ALTER statements run and a later one fails, check which earlier operations succeeded; clearing the log does not undo them.
indexes_edit_7_2: Inspect the success result, updated sidebar and reopened/loaded definition after a create or rename.
indexes_edit_7_3: The app refreshes object navigation and attempts Git object renaming for a renamed index. Git operations are separate from DB DDL; this screen has no general source-history editor.
indexes_edit_description: Oracle permits name and visibility changes here; PostgreSQL permits name changes. Structural replacement is not silently performed for fields that are read-only.
indexes_edit_heading: Edit tab — change an existing index
indexes_intro: An existing index window has three tabs: Edit, Statistics and Source. New indexes open a creation form. Use Edit for supported settings and constraint-aware deletion, Statistics for database-maintained values, and Source for the actual DDL. The tables below distinguish creation-only options from changes allowed on an existing index.
indexes_oracle: Existing Oracle indexes can be renamed or made VISIBLE/INVISIBLE here. Bitmap/reverse/type/key changes are creation settings. Constraint-backed index deletion is blocked; inspect the table constraint first. DDL follows Oracle implicit-commit rules.
indexes_oracle_options_1_2: Enable Bitmap during creation when that index type is appropriate.
indexes_oracle_options_1_3: Adds BITMAP to CREATE INDEX and clears UNIQUE and Reverse in the form. This is not a universal performance improvement; assess the table workload and DB restrictions.
indexes_oracle_options_2_2: Enable Reverse for a supported non-function index during creation.
indexes_oracle_options_2_3: Adds REVERSE and clears Bitmap. Switching to function mode clears Reverse; the DB remains responsible for validating the full option combination.
indexes_oracle_options_3_2: Toggle Visible; on an existing index, review the ALTER preview and click Change.
indexes_oracle_options_3_3: Chooses VISIBLE or INVISIBLE. Invisible is a database index-visibility setting, not hiding the object from MonaBase, and it does not drop the index or remove its maintenance cost.
indexes_oracle_options_4_2: Recheck all checkboxes after enabling UNIQUE, Bitmap, Reverse or function mode.
indexes_oracle_options_4_3: UNIQUE clears Bitmap; Bitmap clears UNIQUE/Reverse; Reverse clears Bitmap. These adjustments avoid some conflicts but do not guarantee that every remaining combination is supported.
indexes_oracle_options_description: These controls are Oracle-specific. Visibility can be changed for an existing index; bitmap/reverse options are creation settings and are not maintenance or rebuild commands.
indexes_oracle_options_heading: Oracle options on the Edit / create form
indexes_postgresql: Existing PostgreSQL editing supports renaming only. Source retains expressions, predicates and other real DDL clauses. Creating a primary key changes a table constraint; deleting its backing index may instead require confirmed constraint removal and is blocked when foreign keys reference it.
indexes_scope_body: Creating an index or constraint is real DDL and can take time or conflict with concurrent activity. Oracle DDL can implicitly commit prior data changes. Existing-index editing intentionally limits supported changes; this form does not offer PostgreSQL access-method/predicate/INCLUDE editing or REBUILD/REINDEX controls. Preserve the full source, constraints and references before planning a structural replacement. A DB operation and any accompanying Git rename/delete are separate results; verify both if repository tracking matters.
indexes_scope_heading: Creation, alteration and maintenance are different
indexes_source_1_2: Read the source fetched through Oracle DBMS_METADATA or PostgreSQL pg_get_indexdef.
indexes_source_1_3: Preserves database details such as expressions and PostgreSQL predicates/INCLUDE/access-method clauses when present, even if the edit form has no field for them.
indexes_source_2_2: Use the copy icon in the source header.
indexes_source_2_3: Copies the fetched DDL without executing it. The separate copy button on Edit copies planned ALTER SQL instead.
indexes_source_3_2: Use the source for inspection or copy it into the SQL window for a separately reviewed change.
indexes_source_3_3: Typing cannot modify source here. A copied CREATE statement is not an automatic replacement or recovery operation for an existing index.
indexes_source_4_2: Compare current Source with the ALTER preview before changing name or Oracle visibility.
indexes_source_4_3: Keeps actual and proposed definitions distinct. Oracle name-plus-visibility changes can consist of several statements; review each console result and fetched state after execution.
indexes_source_description: Available for existing indexes. Source is a read-only database definition, separate from the proposed ALTER preview on Edit. It is not a reconstruction from only the simplified form fields.
indexes_source_heading: Source tab — the actual CREATE definition
indexes_statistics_1_2: Read BLEVEL, LEAF_BLOCKS, DISTINCT_KEYS, NUM_ROWS, SAMPLE_SIZE and LAST_ANALYZED.
indexes_statistics_1_3: Shows tree depth, leaf blocks and collected key/row/sample statistics. Missing or old collection values need not match current table data.
indexes_statistics_2_2: Read index size, idx_scan, idx_tup_read and idx_tup_fetch.
indexes_statistics_2_3: Helps inspect recorded usage. These counters have different meanings and observation/reset periods; a zero is not sufficient reason to delete an index.
indexes_statistics_3_2: Read idx_blks_read/idx_blks_hit and last analyze/autoanalyze/vacuum/autovacuum times.
indexes_statistics_3_3: Shows disk/cache activity plus maintenance times from the related table. These dates are not an index-specific rebuild history.
indexes_statistics_4_2: Read the empty/unfetched indication instead of assuming the statistic is zero.
indexes_statistics_4_3: Means that the particular values were not available. Opening this tab does not run DBMS_STATS, ANALYZE, VACUUM, REBUILD or REINDEX.
indexes_statistics_5_2: For a fresh inspection after external changes, reopen the index window; use Retry if loading failed.
indexes_statistics_5_3: Reloads definition/statistics when the window is initialized again. Merely switching between already-loaded tabs does not continuously refresh DB counters.
indexes_statistics_description: Available for existing indexes. Oracle and PostgreSQL show different fields; these are catalog/counter snapshots, not a live query benchmark or a guarantee that an index is useful.
indexes_step_1: Open the existing index and inspect Source, Statistics and the constraint notice on Edit. For a new index, choose its schema/table and wait for column loading.
indexes_step_2: Review ordered keys or expressions and creation-only options. For an existing index, review the ALTER preview: Oracle supports name/visibility and PostgreSQL supports name changes.
indexes_step_3: Execute the intended operation, inspect each console result and verify the resulting definition. Review constraint-removal effects before deleting and check query plans when assessing performance.
indexes_summary: Inspect index definitions and their dependencies.
indexes_workflow_body: For a new index on an orders table, choose the schema and table, move CUSTOMER_ID and ORDER_DATE into the target list, then place CUSTOMER_ID first and ORDER_DATE second with the order buttons. Check UNIQUE and any Oracle-specific options deliberately, then Create. Inspect Source and Statistics after creation, and use a representative SQL execution plan to verify whether the query actually benefits; key order and an index existing are not proof of faster execution.
materialized_view_logs_intro: An Oracle materialized-view log records changes to a base table for eligible refresh workflows. Review the base table and consumers before changing the log definition.
materialized_view_logs_oracle: This screen is Oracle-only. It is not the application SQL execution log or the stored-program trace log.
materialized_view_logs_step_1: Open the log and confirm the base table and recorded columns.
materialized_view_logs_step_2: Review key, row identity and other available logging attributes together with dependent materialized views.
materialized_view_logs_step_3: Apply supported changes and refresh the information. Check affected refresh workflows before removing a log.
materialized_view_logs_summary: Review change logs that support materialized-view refresh.
materialized_views_intro: Materialized views store query results and can become stale. Inspect the definition, data and refresh information before deciding whether to refresh or change the object.
materialized_views_oracle: Oracle refresh methods and supporting materialized-view logs have specific prerequisites. A requested fast refresh is not guaranteed to be available.
materialized_views_postgresql: PostgreSQL refresh options depend on the object and its indexes. A refresh can hold locks and take time on large datasets.
materialized_views_step_1: Open the materialized view and wait for metadata to finish loading.
materialized_views_step_2: Inspect columns, stored data, dependencies and available refresh settings.
materialized_views_step_3: Review the refresh or definition operation, execute it with suitable privileges, and check the resulting status.
materialized_views_summary: Inspect stored query results and refresh behavior.
mview_detail_common_1_2: Reload the definition and metadata from the database.
mview_detail_common_1_3: Reloads current database values; edited form values may be replaced or trigger a conflict notice.
mview_detail_common_2_2: Discard unsaved changes in the form.
mview_detail_common_2_3: Restores values from the latest loaded definition; does not roll back any executed SQL.
mview_detail_common_3_3: Refreshes stored rows in the database, not merely the on-screen display; operation can take time.
mview_detail_common_4_2: Choose FORCE, COMPLETE or FAST for Refresh now.
mview_detail_common_4_3: Changes the refresh method used for this operation; it does not by itself save a changed definition.
mview_detail_common_5_2: Enable concurrent refresh when metadata says it is available.
mview_detail_common_5_3: Requests CONCURRENTLY for Refresh now; it has database prerequisites and is disabled if unavailable.
mview_detail_common_description: Controls available for an existing materialized view.
mview_detail_console_1_2: Review logged SQL, result messages and errors in the side console.
mview_detail_console_1_3: Helps distinguish an executed database change from a separate Git failure.
mview_detail_console_2_2: Clear console messages or hide the console panel.
mview_detail_console_2_3: Only changes the displayed log panel; does not undo executed operations.
