packages_information_1_2: Use the outlined refresh button or Retry after an information error.
packages_information_1_3: Reloads catalog information without executing a member. A failed retrieval is shown as an error, not as an empty package.
packages_information_2_2: Read each displayed status and AUTHID value for the package.
packages_information_2_3: Distinguishes specification/body validity and execution-rights mode. Viewing the values does not change rights or compile an invalid body.
packages_information_3_2: Inspect members listed with their argument-type signatures.
packages_information_3_3: Lets you distinguish same-name declarations. This catalog list is not a source-level inventory of every private helper in the body.
packages_information_4_2: Read name/type, IN/OUT, function return type and default availability for each member.
packages_information_4_3: Describes the declared contract, not runtime values. A user-defined type may be displayed even when the execution panel cannot handle it; default availability is not the full default expression.
packages_information_5_2: Read each object’s owner, name and type before changing the public interface or deleting the package.
packages_information_5_3: Provides visible direct dependencies for impact review. It does not automatically fix callers after a signature change.
packages_information_6_2: Treat the lists as catalog-visible direct links, not all external calls or a complete recursive graph.
packages_information_6_3: Dynamic SQL, application calls and inaccessible objects can be absent. An empty list does not prove that a package is safe to delete.
packages_information_description: Both specification and body windows expose the package-level information view. This is read-only metadata, separate from editing and from the runtime argument values.
packages_information_heading: Information tab — status, members and dependencies
packages_intro: Oracle packages have a specification (PACKAGE) and implementation body (PACKAGE BODY). Existing objects show Source, Version control and Information; a recorded body also offers Trace analysis. The tables below explain the controls, member selection and argument settings, distinguishing DB changes from source history and trace replay.
packages_members_1_2: Choose the intended member, such as HELLO(NUMBER) versus HELLO(VARCHAR2), rather than relying only on the name.
packages_members_1_3: Loads that member’s arguments and scrolls toward its source. Switching targets resets input modes/values, return results and current trace replay to avoid reusing another member’s state.
packages_members_2_2: Inspect types before execution. This panel supports scalar families such as NUMBER, VARCHAR2, DATE and TIMESTAMP.
packages_members_2_3: Unsupported object/record/collection, cursor or other types can block execution, including unsupported return types. Use the SQL window for a separately prepared invocation.
packages_members_3_2: Enter IN or IN/OUT values; leave a field empty only when SQL NULL is intended.
packages_members_3_3: Blank/missing input becomes NULL. Whitespace and the text null are explicit values, not a request to use a parameter default.
packages_members_4_2: For a defaulted argument select default mode; for an explicit date use the input example or calendar.
packages_members_4_3: Default mode disables the input and omits that argument. Date input is converted with type information; supported numeric fields are checked before execution.
packages_members_5_2: Use Retry for the currently selected target if its argument load fails.
packages_members_5_3: Keeps execution/trace disabled until the selected member’s arguments load successfully. It does not silently treat a read failure as a no-argument routine.
packages_members_6_2: After verifying the target, validity and inputs, click Execute.
packages_members_6_3: Runs the DB-installed member with typed arguments, not an uncompiled draft. Package initialization/state and member code can affect results or data.
packages_members_7_2: Read the lower results after a function/procedure completes. Pure OUT and function return values are outputs, not input fields.
packages_members_7_3: Shows available returned/output values. An empty output list does not prove that the routine made no changes.
packages_members_8_2: Read DBMS_OUTPUT, compilation diagnostics and execution errors; use the trash icon only when finished with the current analysis.
packages_members_8_3: In the package window, clear log also clears the current replay and trace timestamp display, hiding its trace tab. It does not undo DB work or mean that saved trace files were deleted.
packages_members_description: Available on an existing body. The target label includes argument types so overloaded members remain distinguishable; the selected member’s internal identity is used to load its exact arguments.
packages_members_heading: Source tab — select a member and set arguments
packages_oracle: Package state and initialization can influence repeated executions in a session. A valid specification does not guarantee a valid body.
packages_parts_1_2: Open the specification from the package’s sidebar entries.
packages_parts_1_3: Edits the public declarations. This screen does not show member execution controls or trace acquisition for the specification.
packages_parts_2_2: Open the body to edit implementation and run a supported public member.
packages_parts_2_3: Adds target selection and argument/result panels. Member availability comes from the loaded package metadata, not every private local routine in the source.
packages_parts_3_2: Start the selected kind with its template and edit the package name in that schema. Create the required specification before a matching body.
packages_parts_3_3: Initially exposes source editing; compile success identifies the newly created object. Creating a body does not automatically create or synchronize its specification.
packages_parts_4_2: Inspect PACKAGE and PACKAGE BODY status in Information before executing members.
packages_parts_4_3: A valid specification alone is insufficient for body execution. Invalid status prompts compilation/diagnostic review rather than treating the package as ready.
packages_parts_description: Oracle-only. Existing packages have Source, Version control and Information; a body with a recording also offers Trace analysis. The specification and body are separate editing targets, not two interchangeable source drafts.
packages_parts_heading: Choose the specification or body first
packages_scope_body: Package initialization and session state can influence repeated member runs. Running or recording a trace can have side effects; replay only inspects an existing run. Oracle DDL can implicitly commit pending work, and member code can perform its own transaction control or external work. Review the actual environment and results. Source AI assistance and trace AI investigation use the configured provider and prepared context; generated code still needs your review/compilation, and AI receives no direct DB connection.
packages_scope_heading: State, data changes and AI assistance
packages_source_1_2: Edit the full definition with line numbers and completion for SQL/PLSQL, DB objects and local symbols.
packages_source_1_3: Changes the draft. The Source asterisk signals a difference from the loaded/compiled baseline; it is not an automatic DB save or Git commit.
packages_source_2_2: Keep the opened schema/name and PACKAGE versus PACKAGE BODY kind, then click Compile.
packages_source_2_3: Executes the definition on the main DB connection and checks compilation diagnostics. A different target/kind is rejected; success clears trace replay and reloads the existing object.
packages_source_3_2: Read marked source positions and the lower console after compilation.
packages_source_3_3: Compilation errors block a clean success. Warnings are displayed separately and can remain after successful compilation; checking only a success message is insufficient for a full review.
packages_source_4_2: Use Retry in the definition error and wait for source/status metadata to load.
packages_source_4_3: Reloads required metadata while preserving an existing edited draft. Normal member execution requires both valid definition state and matching loaded arguments.
packages_source_5_2: Configure AI, open the source AI button and describe the intended specification/body change and relevant references.
packages_source_5_3: Prepares coding assistance for the selected part. Review generated/applied source, check the other part and compile deliberately; AI does not directly connect to the DB.
packages_source_6_2: Use Delete only after checking which part is open and the confirmation.
packages_source_6_3: Issues DROP PACKAGE or DROP PACKAGE BODY. Deleting a package member is not what this button does; trace/Git cleanup is attempted separately from DB deletion.
packages_source_7_2: On the body, open/close the argument panel; drag the boundaries to adjust source/result space.
packages_source_7_3: Changes layout only. Execution, compilation and AI preparation disable conflicting actions while busy.
packages_source_8_2: Inspect the refreshed object and record the reviewed specification/body from Version control when needed.
packages_source_8_3: DB compilation and Git recording are separate. Do not assume both parts or their Git history were synchronized just because one compile succeeded.
packages_source_description: Edit only the opened specification or body. Public declarations and implementations must remain compatible; saving one part is not a complete migration of the whole package and its callers.
packages_source_heading: Source tab — edit and compile the selected part
packages_step_1: Open the specification/body as intended and inspect both statuses, member signatures and dependencies in Information. Preserve current source before changing it.
packages_step_2: Compile the intended definitions, select the exact member on the body, load its arguments, choose explicit values/NULL/defaults and execute in a suitable environment.
packages_step_3: Inspect outputs/diagnostics, acquire and replay a fresh trace when needed, and record the reviewed specification/body in Git. Use the trace guide for detailed debugging.
packages_summary: Work with PL/SQL specifications, bodies and members.
packages_trace_1_2: Choose a member and inputs on Source, then use Execute trace in a suitable test environment.
packages_trace_1_3: Executes the supported instrumented program and records its steps/values. It can have real side effects, unlike replaying an existing recording.
packages_trace_2_2: Resolve the Source asterisk before acquiring a trace; inspect specification/body validity and argument readiness.
packages_trace_2_3: Tracing an unsaved package draft is rejected. Acquisition uses the DB-saved definition, avoiding a misleading recording for uncompiled text.
packages_trace_3_2: Check the selected member, analysis time and recorded arguments before investigating.
packages_trace_3_3: Target changes clear current playback. A saved recording is restored only when the app can associate it safely; do not assume all overloads share one compatible trace.
packages_trace_4_2: Use Play to start or Resume after a replay pause.
packages_trace_4_3: Moves through recorded execution without invoking the package again. A freshness check can reject an old recording after definition changes.
packages_trace_5_2: Step through captured events or stop replay from the debug toolbar.
packages_trace_5_3: Changes the analysis position only. Stopping replay is not rollback or cancellation of the original DB execution.
packages_trace_6_2: Toggle a margin breakpoint and right-click for hit count or variable comparison conditions.
packages_trace_6_3: Controls where playback pauses when recorded events match; it does not change the member’s stored code.
packages_trace_7_2: Use right-side variables and arguments, any available Conditions tab, and source search while replaying.
packages_trace_7_3: Shows recorded snapshots and inputs. Missing values are not proof of NULL; a source-text match is not proof that a line executed.
packages_trace_8_1: Ask AI to analyze the trace
packages_trace_8_2: With AI configured, use the trace AI button, review prepared context and state the observed issue. Confirm large-data requests when offered.
packages_trace_8_3: Prepares trace evidence and current source for AI reasoning. The AI does not attach to a DB debugger or execute package members directly.
packages_trace_description: Available only on a body with trace data. Acquisition and replay are different operations. For detailed steps, supported programs and limitations, see the [Trace analysis guide](/monabase/guides/trace/).
packages_trace_heading: Trace analysis tab — record and replay a member
packages_trace_workflow_body: Use representative inputs in a dedicated environment and compile pending edits before acquisition. Confirm the exact member, acquire the trace, inspect its timestamp/arguments, then replay with breakpoints and recorded values. Switching members or clearing package logs resets the current replay; a source change also needs a new recording for verification. For detailed acquisition/replay steps and supported-program limitations, see the [Trace analysis guide](/monabase/guides/trace/).
packages_trace_workflow_heading: From package execution to trace replay
packages_version_1_2: Inspect/copy the current editor text for the selected part.
packages_version_1_3: May include uncompiled edits. Copying a specification does not include its body or restore package data/state.
packages_version_2_2: Use the refresh icon to reload source/status/member information.
packages_version_2_3: Preserves an existing edited draft and retains the selected member when possible. Refresh does not silently discard all edits.
packages_version_3_2: Record the reviewed part with a useful message; configured AI can help summarize its changes.
packages_version_3_3: Creates a local source-history commit. Record specification/body consistently when an interface change needs both; committing does not compile either part into the DB.
packages_version_4_2: Select a revision, compare two revisions or review schema-level source changes.
packages_version_4_3: Shows source differences without executing them. Review the public interface and implementation together, not only a member’s changed lines.
packages_version_5_2: Select the intended version and open its SQL for review.
packages_version_5_3: Prepares SQL rather than automatically restoring a package. Plan specification/body order and dependent objects; it does not reverse prior member data changes.
packages_version_6_2: Check the configured repository/remote before Push; reload Git state when needed.
packages_version_6_3: Sends source commits or reads repository state. It does not deploy both package parts to another Oracle database.
packages_version_description: Set up local Git before recording. The shared view receives the currently opened PACKAGE or PACKAGE BODY source, so check both object kind and draft state.
packages_version_heading: Version control tab — specification/body source history
packages_workflow_body: Inspect specification and body together, record their current source, and review member signatures in Information. Modify the intended implementation, compile the necessary parts and inspect status/diagnostics. On the body, select HELLO(NUMBER) or HELLO(VARCHAR2) deliberately, re-enter the inputs and verify RETURN/OUT and DBMS_OUTPUT. A successful compile and a successful member run are separate checks; record the reviewed specification/body after verification.
packages_workflow_heading: Example: change an overloaded package member
privacy_ai_body: AI features are optional and require configuration. When you explicitly request an AI operation, prompts and any included SQL, source code, schema information, trace information or other context are sent to the configured AI endpoint, which may be a third-party service or an endpoint you operate. Review the send preview and remove confidential or personal data before sending. Handling, retention, model training and cross-border processing by that endpoint are governed by its provider and your agreement with it. MonaBase does not control those provider practices.
privacy_analytics_body: This website uses Google Analytics 4 (measurement ID: G-2MV9LLEF3H) to understand page views and traffic sources and improve the documentation. On a first visit, the site requests your consent. Until you accept, it does not download Google Analytics tags or transmit analytics information to that service. Declining does not prevent use of the site. After consent, Google may use cookies and process information such as pages viewed, access times, device/browser information, referral sources, online identifiers, and information associated with IP addresses. Google may process this data in other countries. This website configures Google Signals and ad-personalization signals as disabled. Your choice is saved in browser local storage and can be changed using the “Analytics settings” control. Changing to Decline stops analytics tag loading on subsequent page loads after a reload; it does not automatically delete information already transmitted. You can also clear browser cookies and site data. See [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy).
privacy_changes_body: This policy may be updated when MonaBase features, data flows, third-party integrations or legal requirements change. The latest version will be published on this page with an updated revision date.
privacy_choices_body: You decide which databases and external endpoints to connect to, whether to enable and use AI, what to include in prompts, and whether to push to remote Git. You can review and change configured connections, credentials and settings, manage relevant histories within supported functions, and remove locally stored app data through the application or operating system as appropriate. Removing local files does not erase copies already sent to database, AI or Git services; use those services’ controls separately.
privacy_data_body: Depending on your actions, MonaBase processes connection names, hostnames, ports, database names, usernames, authentication secrets, SQL statements, query results, database object definitions, diagnostic traces, Git repository information, editor content, settings, and AI prompts/responses. These may contain personal or confidential information. Data is accessed to deliver the features you use, rather than for an unrelated purpose.
privacy_database_body: When you connect to an Oracle or PostgreSQL database, connection parameters and your requested SQL/operations are transmitted to that database, directly or through an SSH tunnel if configured. The database server and its administrator may record SQL, access logs and query results according to their own configuration. MonaBase does not make an external database read-only merely by displaying read-only mode: enforce appropriate database account privileges as well.
privacy_git_body: Git features may write database object definitions, ER-diagram metadata, diffs, and commit messages to your configured local repository. When you push or pull, relevant repository data and authentication traffic pass between your device and the selected remote Git service. Avoid committing passwords, database records and other secrets. Remote retention and access controls depend on the service and repository permissions.
privacy_intro: This privacy policy explains data handling for the MonaBase desktop application and its project website.
privacy_retention_body: Locally retained information remains until it is changed, overwritten or deleted by you, an app function, or the operating system; actual file retention varies by feature. The app sends information to third parties only when the corresponding configured workflow makes the request. Remote recipients and retention depend on your selected service. Use limited-permission credentials, secure endpoints, device encryption and access controls; no technical system can guarantee absolute security.
privacy_rights_body: For privacy-related questions or requests, use the [Contact & Support page](../contact/). Public [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/eijiikemura/monabase/issues) and [Discussions](https://github.com/eijiikemura/monabase/discussions) are visible to others. For non-public general inquiries, use [X direct messages to @eijiikemura](https://x.com/eijiikemura). An X account is required, but message requests are accepted from all accounts regardless of follow status. Requests are screened with spam filters and reviewed as appropriate; replies are not guaranteed. Security vulnerabilities should use [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/eijiikemura/monabase/security) rather than public Issues. No email or private web-form contact service is provided, and people without X have no alternative private general-inquiry channel through this project. Never send credentials, database content or unnecessary personal data. GitHub and X independently process accounts, messages and attachments under their own policies. Requests concerning information held by AI providers, database operators, Git services, hosting providers or Microsoft should be directed to the relevant service where appropriate.
privacy_scope_body: This policy applies to MonaBase, a desktop database development and administration tool distributed by the MonaBase project. The application is developed by eiji ikemura. This policy describes information handled by the desktop application and the linked website. It does not replace the policies of your database operator, AI provider, Git remote, or Microsoft Store. Last updated: November 1, 2026.
privacy_storage_body: MonaBase stores connection profiles, app settings, SQL history, AI usage records and certain conversation histories in files on your device. Supported credential fields use the operating system-backed Electron safeStorage encryption when available; secrets that cannot be securely persisted may need to be re-entered. Local files and exported data remain subject to device access, backup and file-permission risks. Do not assume every saved file is encrypted.
privacy_summary: How MonaBase handles local data, database connections, AI, Git and third-party services.
privacy_telemetry_body: The inspected application code includes local AI token usage history and local diagnostic/history functions. This policy does not claim that every network request is absent or that all future versions are telemetry-free. If optional crash reporting, analytics or update checks are introduced, the actual implementation and this policy must be reviewed and updated before release.
privacy_website_body: The project website may be hosted on GitHub Pages. The hosting provider may process access logs and technical identifiers under its own policies. If you obtain MonaBase via Microsoft Store, Microsoft may process installation, distribution and diagnostic information under its own terms. For contact and support, MonaBase links to third-party GitHub Issues, Discussions, private vulnerability reporting, and X direct messages. X message requests are accepted from all accounts and screened with spam filters. Opening and using these platforms subjects account, message and attachment data to GitHub or X privacy terms. MonaBase does not operate an email or contact-form support service.
query_builder_add_effect: Adds cards with the objects’ column names to the canvas. Already-added objects are excluded from duplicate addition. The objects are used as query sources; they are not copied or created in the database.
query_builder_add_how: Choose a schema and Table or View, search by name and browse in pages of 100. Select objects and confirm the addition.
query_builder_agg_avg_effect: Computes the average over non-NULL values per group. NULL rows do not count as zero.
query_builder_agg_avg_how: Choose AVG on a suitable numeric column.
query_builder_agg_count_effect: Counts non-NULL values per group. In a LEFT join, counting a right-hand key can show 0 when there is no matching record.
query_builder_agg_count_how: Choose COUNT on a column whose non-NULL values you want to count.
query_builder_agg_group_effect: Returns a group for each distinct combination of grouping values. Grouping several columns makes the grouping more detailed.
query_builder_agg_group_how: Select Grouping for a key such as customer name or category.
query_builder_agg_max_effect: Returns the maximum non-NULL value in each group, according to database type and comparison rules.
query_builder_agg_max_how: Choose MAX on the value to compare.
query_builder_agg_min_effect: Returns the minimum non-NULL value in each group.
query_builder_agg_min_how: Choose MIN on the value to compare.
query_builder_agg_none_effect: Selects the original column. If another field introduces aggregation, shown non-aggregate columns are grouped.
query_builder_agg_none_how: Leave aggregation unset on the field.
query_builder_agg_sum_effect: Computes the sum within each group. Join multiplication can inflate the sum, so check the join’s row relationships.
query_builder_agg_sum_how: Choose SUM for a suitable numeric column, such as order amount.
query_builder_aggregate_effect: Changes the selected expression or grouping. Choosing an aggregate automatically groups other shown, non-aggregated fields. Check all fields when changing or removing aggregation.
query_builder_aggregate_how: Choose None, Grouping, SUM, COUNT, MAX, MIN or AVG.
query_builder_aggregates_description: Filters apply to source rows before aggregation. COUNT is COUNT(column), not COUNT(*), and ignores NULL values. HAVING is not available in this grid.
query_builder_ai_button_effect: Prepares the selected sources’ definitions and the current design for the AI sidebar. A valid proposal is reviewed before applying; it is not executed automatically. Detailed steps follow below.
query_builder_ai_button_how: Add at least one table/view, enable the provider in AI Settings, then click the AI button.
query_builder_ai_example_body: Assuming CUSTOMERS and ORDERS with a customer key, customer name, order status and numeric amount: “Join customers to orders on the customer key. Show customer name and SUM of amount for PAID orders, grouped by customer name and sorted by the sum descending. Include only customers with matching orders. Use only the sources already added; ask if a column is unclear.” After applying, verify the INNER join, the status condition, customer-name grouping, SUM and DESC. If several customers share a name, add a customer identifier to the grouping to keep them separate.
query_builder_ai_review_body: The review shows before/after SQL and expandable table/field/join/condition settings. The response must reference existing columns in the sources you provided and fit the builder’s supported settings. Plain explanations or clarification questions do not replace the design. Before applying, the app reads definitions again; if the design or reference definitions changed, request a fresh proposal. Applied settings can be revised manually or undone through design history. AI receives context supplied by MonaBase, not direct database access.
query_builder_ai_review_title: Reviewing and applying an AI proposal
query_builder_ai_steps_body:
1. Enable and configure the provider in AI Settings. Add the tables/views the query may use; the AI button requires at least one source.
2. Click the builder’s AI button. The app retrieves fresh definitions, column types/comments and the current design, then opens the sidebar. Row data is not part of this prepared reference package.
3. Describe the desired output, filters, totals, sorting and which unmatched records should remain. Add exact column names when comments or logical names are ambiguous.
4. Optionally use Preview request, then click Send. If the AI asks a clarification question, answer it before expecting a design proposal.
5. A valid structured answer opens a before/after review. Read the SQL and settings, then choose Apply to design or Discard.
6. After applying, check the design and click Execute yourself. Applying the proposal does not run SQL.
query_builder_ai_steps_title: Ask AI to build or adjust the query
query_builder_buttons_description: Hover over icon buttons to see their tooltips. The builder creates a SELECT from the diagram and grid settings; editing the design does not execute it.
query_builder_canvas_description: Source cards occupy the upper canvas; output fields and settings occupy the lower Design grid. You can resize their areas by dragging the divider.
query_builder_clear_effect: Removes all tables, fields and joins from the current design. It does not drop tables or delete database rows. Use Undo if you want to restore the design before another operation resets its history.
query_builder_clear_how: Click Clear and confirm the message.
query_builder_conditions_example_body: For STATUS, set Condition = 'PAID' and OR = 'PENDING'. For AMOUNT, set Condition >= 200. The combined filter means (STATUS = 'PAID' OR STATUS = 'PENDING') AND AMOUNT >= 200. If AMOUNT also uses SUM, the filter still removes individual rows below 200 before summing; it does not mean SUM(AMOUNT) >= 200. Aggregated-result filtering needs HAVING in a SQL window.
query_builder_conditions_example_title: How AND, OR and aggregation combine
query_builder_criteria_effect: Adds a WHERE condition on the source column. Include operators and quote string literals yourself. Conditions on different fields are joined with AND.
query_builder_criteria_how: Enter the part after the column name, for example >= 200, = 'PAID', LIKE '%Tokyo%', IN ('PAID', 'PENDING') or IS NULL.
query_builder_execute_effect: Runs the generated SELECT and opens Results / logs. See returned rows and the SQL in Execution log; changing the design later does not automatically refresh the result. With tables but no grid fields, SELECT * is generated.
query_builder_execute_how: Finish the design and click the green Execute button. Resolve any displayed validation error first.
query_builder_field_add_effect: Adds a field with Show checked and no aggregation, sort or filter. The same source column is not added twice through this action.
query_builder_field_add_how: Double-click a column in a source card, or drag it into the lower Design grid.
query_builder_field_order_effect: Changes output-column order and sort-key priority. Removing a field also removes that field’s filtering/sorting/grouping settings; it does not drop the database column.
query_builder_field_order_how: Drag a grid field horizontally to change its position; use its × button to remove it.
query_builder_fields_description: Each vertical field column has an origin, aggregation, sort, Show, Condition and OR setting. These settings jointly determine the generated SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and ORDER BY.
query_builder_intro: Arrange tables/views and choose fields, joins, filters, aggregates and ordering to build a SELECT visually. The tables below explain each control and how it changes the query. Undo/redo supports design exploration, JSON saving is optional, and execution is always an explicit step.
query_builder_join_disconnected_effect: Independent source groups become CROSS JOINs, producing combinations of their rows. A missing join can greatly increase row counts and totals.
query_builder_join_disconnected_how: Check that every intended relationship is represented before Execute.
query_builder_join_drag_effect: Creates an equality join, initially INNER. Check the table/column pair and join type in Join conditions. It does not create a foreign-key constraint.
query_builder_join_drag_how: Drag one source column onto a column in another card. Start with one selected column for clarity.
query_builder_join_inner_effect: Returns only rows that match on both sides. Unmatched records are omitted.
query_builder_join_left_effect: Keeps Table 1 rows and uses NULL for unmatched Table 2 values. A WHERE condition on Table 2 may still remove those unmatched rows.
query_builder_join_left_how: Choose Left outer join to keep all rows from Table 1.
query_builder_join_multi_effect: Combines the equality comparisons with AND in one ON clause. Conflicting join types for the same pair are rejected.
query_builder_join_multi_how: Add another column pair between the same two tables and use a consistent join direction/type.
query_builder_join_pair_effect: Generates an equality comparison in ON. Check the meaning and types yourself; similarly named columns are not necessarily related.
query_builder_join_pair_how: Select the two sources and their corresponding columns, for example CUSTOMERS.ID and ORDERS.CUSTOMER_ID.
query_builder_join_remove_effect: Removes that design condition. It does not drop a database constraint; removing the last link can turn sources into a CROSS JOIN.
query_builder_join_remove_how: Use the trash icon on the join row.
query_builder_join_right_effect: Keeps Table 2 rows and uses NULL for unmatched Table 1 values. Review filtering on the optional side.
query_builder_join_right_how: Choose Right outer join to keep all rows from Table 2.
query_builder_joins_description: Use the Join conditions tab to review each pair. “Table 1” and “Table 2” identify the join’s configured ends; they are not determined by which card happens to be drawn on the left or right.
query_builder_limits_body: The builder supports equality joins (INNER/LEFT/RIGHT), multiple keys between a pair and independent join groups. Self-joins using repeated copies of the same source, cyclic joins, HAVING, subqueries in conditions and arbitrary expression editing are outside this UI. Invalid designs show an error instead of executing guessed SQL. For advanced queries, take executed SQL from the log/history and continue in a SQL window. Saving a builder JSON is optional and is separate from saving .sql text.
query_builder_limits_title: When to use a SQL window instead
query_builder_load_effect: Replaces the current design and resets its Undo history after validating the file. Oracle and PostgreSQL documents must match the current database type. Loading does not run SQL; verify the referenced objects exist on the current connection.
query_builder_load_how: Use the upload/read icon to open a saved query-builder JSON file.
query_builder_move_effect: Changes the visual layout and saved card position. It does not change join direction or the meaning of the query.
query_builder_multi_effect: Adds the selected columns without repeatedly dragging one at a time. Selecting a column alone does not add it to the output.
query_builder_multi_how: Use Ctrl (Cmd on macOS) to toggle columns; Shift selects a range in the same card. Drag the selected columns to the grid together.
query_builder_note: A drawn join changes the query, not the database foreign keys. Check joins and row counts before relying on totals.
query_builder_or_effect: Produces (column = 'PAID' OR column = 'PENDING'). It does not OR the whole row of conditions across unrelated fields.
query_builder_or_how: Enter an alternative condition for the same field, such as = 'PENDING' after Condition = 'PAID'.
query_builder_origin_effect: Identifies which table/view supplies the value. These labels are not free-form expression or alias editors.
query_builder_origin_how: Read the column name and source name at the top of each field. To use a different source column, remove the field and add the intended one.
query_builder_pg_schema_effect: Updates the builder’s schema selection. Existing cards retain their schema-qualified names; selecting a different schema does not replace them with similarly named tables.
query_builder_pg_schema_how: Choose the schema from the selector in the PostgreSQL builder. You can also choose a schema in Add.
query_builder_redo_effect: Reapplies the design change you undid. A new design edit starts a different path and clears the redo states.
query_builder_redo_how: Click the right-curved arrow after Undo.
query_builder_remove_source_effect: Removes that source and its dependent fields and joins from the design. The underlying table/view remains in the database.
query_builder_remove_source_how: Click × in the source card header.
query_builder_results_body: After Execute, open Results / logs to inspect rows, errors and the generated SQL in Execution log. The normal result controls include transpose, cell inspection and clipboard/CSV/Excel export of fetched results. History can open executed SQL in a SQL window. There is no always-visible SQL editor in the design canvas: manual SQL work or plan-based tuning belongs in a SQL window, while AI proposals show SQL in their review dialog. Redesigning the query does not rerun it or refresh existing rows.
query_builder_save_effect: Saves tables, positions, fields, joins, conditions and schema context as JSON for optional reuse. It is not a SQL file or result export, and it does not change database definitions.
query_builder_save_how: Use the download/save icon and choose a destination; the default filename is query-builder.json.
query_builder_show_effect: Controls the SELECT output, not whether the field exists in the design. If fields are present, at least one must be shown; hiding all fields is a validation error.
query_builder_show_how: Check to include a field in the result; uncheck to use it only for supported filtering/sorting/grouping.
query_builder_sort_effect: Adds ORDER BY; an aggregated field sorts by the aggregated value. Without explicit ordering, row order is not guaranteed.
query_builder_sort_how: Choose None, ASC or DESC. For several sort keys, order the fields from left to right by priority.
query_builder_step_1: Use Add to choose a schema and tables or views. Search and browse the selector in pages of 100 objects.
query_builder_step_2: Add fields and configure joins, filters, grouping and ordering using the tables above. Review the AI before/after dialog when using a proposal; executed SQL is available in Execution log.
query_builder_step_3: Click Execute and inspect the rows and log. Use configured AI support to request a reviewed design proposal, or optionally load/save JSON to reuse the layout.
query_builder_summary: Build a SELECT visually from tables and views.
query_builder_undo_effect: Restores a previous design state, including fields, conditions, joins and layout. It does not undo database operations. Design history retains up to 100 previous states.
query_builder_undo_how: Click the left-curved arrow after changing the design.
sequences_information_1_2: Use the outlined refresh button or Retry for information errors.
sequences_information_1_3: Reloads settings/usage metadata without calling NEXTVAL/nextval or changing settings inputs.
sequences_information_2_2: Read NUMBER on Oracle or smallint/integer/bigint on PostgreSQL, plus effective limits/cache/options.
sequences_information_2_3: Shows loaded DB settings rather than unapplied edits. The form preserves an existing PostgreSQL type; it does not offer a type-conversion selector.
sequences_information_3_2: Read the same cache/unknown note as on Settings.
sequences_information_3_3: Is a metadata observation, not a guaranteed next value or proof that no other consumer has advanced numbering.
sequences_information_4_2: On PostgreSQL inspect the table/column association and any IDENTITY marker.
sequences_information_4_3: Describes a column relationship rather than the sequence’s login/role owner. Oracle has no PostgreSQL-style OWNED BY association in this view; None does not mean unused.
sequences_information_5_2: Read visible direct catalog references before deletion or restart.
sequences_information_5_3: Helps review recorded dependencies, but dynamic SQL, indirect links and application consumers may be absent. It is not an inventory of every issued ID.
sequences_information_description: Information reads current catalog metadata separately from the settings draft. It provides inspection controls, not a way to edit ownership or allocate the next number.
sequences_information_heading: Information tab — type, ownership and dependencies
sequences_intro: Existing sequence windows have Settings, Source and Information tabs; new sequences show a creation form. They distinguish metadata reference values, local restart candidates and actual DB numbering. The tables below explain common settings, Oracle options, explicit restart and safe review of concurrent changes.
sequences_note: Restarting can create values that conflict with existing rows. Sequence values should not be treated as a gap-free counter.
sequences_oracle: Restart support depends on the Oracle version. Unsupported or unverifiable versions disable restart while allowing valid ordinary setting changes.
sequences_oracle_1_2: Toggle ORDER when sequence generation must follow request order.
sequences_oracle_1_3: Requests DB ordering; it is not commit order or gapless numbering. SESSION disables this setting.
sequences_oracle_2_2: Choose KEEP for the intended Oracle Application Continuity replay behavior.
sequences_oracle_2_3: Concerns NEXTVAL reuse during qualifying DB replay, subject to ownership/privileges. It is unrelated to MonaBase trace replay or preserving the current UI candidate.
sequences_oracle_3_2: Toggle SESSION for a session sequence rather than the normal GLOBAL behavior.
sequences_oracle_3_3: Uses session-local sequence state. CACHE/ORDER are ignored by Oracle and disabled in the form; this is not a globally unique numbering policy.
sequences_oracle_description: ORDER, KEEP and SESSION are available on the Oracle form. They are DB sequence clauses, not display preferences; effective behavior depends on the DB feature, privileges and environment.
sequences_postgresql: PostgreSQL sequence data types and OWNED BY relationships are preserved in source inspection. A sequence can depend on a table column.
sequences_restart_1_2: Read the read-only value and cache note; unknown can be shown when metadata has no usable value.
sequences_restart_1_3: May represent a cache boundary or be overtaken by other connections. It is not a promise of the next number any application will receive.
sequences_restart_2_2: Enter the intended integer for an existing sequence, then review range and possible reuse.
sequences_restart_2_3: Changes a local candidate and enables the separate restart action when supported. It does not execute SQL by typing or by ordinary settings Save.
sequences_restart_3_2: Use the button next to the restart target to add the currently entered increment to that candidate.
sequences_restart_3_3: Performs exact local integer arithmetic. It does not obtain the next sequence value, consume a number or change the DB sequence.
sequences_restart_4_2: Press Restart only after changing a candidate and confirm the named schema/sequence, value and latest observed reference.
sequences_restart_4_3: Validates against current DB settings and executes ALTER SEQUENCE RESTART. It does not save other unsaved limit/step edits or update existing table IDs.
sequences_restart_5_2: Read the support message if Restart is disabled. Reload settings to retry version detection.
sequences_restart_5_3: MonaBase enables native restart when it identifies Oracle 18 or later; older/unknown versions keep restart disabled while supported setting changes remain separate. It does not emulate restart by recreating the object.
sequences_restart_6_2: Review existing IDs and other sequence consumers before confirming a restart.
sequences_restart_6_3: Issued numbers can be issued again after restart or cycle. The app does not synchronize every caller or prove uniqueness against every consuming table.
sequences_restart_description: Reading metadata does not call NEXTVAL/nextval. Treat the observed value, local restart candidate and actual DB restart as three different things.
sequences_restart_heading: Settings tab — reference value and explicit restart
sequences_review_1_2: Use Refresh in settings, or Retry after metadata retrieval fails.
sequences_review_1_3: Reloads metadata/support information without numbering. An edited settings draft keeps its original baseline so conflicts remain detectable; operations stay blocked until metadata is ready.
sequences_review_2_2: Use the reload/discard button and confirm that you want to discard edited settings.
sequences_review_2_3: Replaces the settings draft with DB values. The separately touched restart candidate is retained, so review it before any later restart.
sequences_review_3_2: Read the original/latest/your values if another connection changed the same field.
sequences_review_3_3: Stops that save for review. Nonconflicting changes can be merged with the latest DB definition rather than overwriting unrelated settings.
sequences_review_4_1: Keep my changes for the next save
sequences_review_4_2: Use this action only after deciding to keep your edited settings, then Save again.
sequences_review_4_3: Adopts the reviewed latest baseline and keeps intended local differences. The button itself executes no ALTER; the next Save rechecks the DB again.
sequences_review_description: For an existing sequence, settings Save compares the loaded baseline, your edits and the latest DB settings. Changing a display reference or a different connection’s numbering does not itself mean the sequence must be recreated.
sequences_review_heading: Settings tab — refresh and concurrent changes
sequences_safety_body: Sequence allocation, cached values, concurrent callers and table transactions are distinct. Disabling cache or enabling ORDER is not a gapless-numbering or duplicate-cleanup mechanism. Restart/cycle can reuse numbers, while saving settings does not repair existing rows or coordinate every caller. Review the actual environment and dependencies; Oracle DDL can implicitly commit pending work. For DB clause semantics see [Oracle CREATE SEQUENCE](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/sqlrf/CREATE-SEQUENCE.html) and [PostgreSQL 16 CREATE SEQUENCE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createsequence.html).
sequences_safety_heading: Numbering is not gapless data recovery
sequences_settings_10_2: Use integer literals for step, bounds, cache and start/restart values.
sequences_settings_10_3: Rejects decimals, SQL fragments and invalid ranges before execution. Large integer values are handled without ordinary floating-point rounding.
sequences_settings_1_2: Enter a name when creating. Existing names are read-only; creation normalizes Oracle names to uppercase and PostgreSQL names to lowercase.
sequences_settings_1_3: Chooses the sequence created in the selected schema. This form does not rename an existing sequence.
sequences_settings_2_2: For creation only, enter a starting integer within the chosen limits and direction.
sequences_settings_2_3: Sets the initial start for CREATE SEQUENCE. Existing numbering is moved only by the separate Restart action.
sequences_settings_3_2: Enter a nonzero integer, positive for ascending or negative for descending numbering.
sequences_settings_3_3: Changes the step for subsequent numbering after save. Recheck default limits and the creation start when changing sign.
sequences_settings_4_2: Choose an explicit minimum or the no-explicit-limit option.
sequences_settings_4_3: Default bounds depend on DB, increment direction and PostgreSQL sequence data type; no-explicit-limit does not mean unlimited arbitrary integers.
sequences_settings_5_2: Choose an explicit maximum or the no-explicit-limit option. Keep maximum greater than minimum.
sequences_settings_5_3: Sets the upper bound used by validation and subsequent numbering; start/restart values must lie within the applicable range.
sequences_settings_6_2: Choose caching and an integer size. Oracle uses NOCACHE when disabled; PostgreSQL uses CACHE 1.
sequences_settings_6_3: Controls preallocated numbers, not table rows. The form checks DB-specific sizes; Oracle SESSION ignores cache and disables these controls.
sequences_settings_7_2: Enable only when reuse after reaching a bound is intended.
sequences_settings_7_3: Ascending numbering wraps to the minimum and descending to the maximum. This is not duplicate detection against existing table data.
sequences_settings_8_2: Review the name, start, limits and options, then use Create in the new form.
sequences_settings_8_3: Executes CREATE SEQUENCE and changes the window/navigation to the created object. PostgreSQL creation uses bigint here; this form has no data-type selector.
sequences_settings_9_2: Edit only the settings you want and click Save.
sequences_settings_9_3: Rechecks the latest definition and applies supported ALTER clauses. It does not drop/recreate the sequence or apply the separate restart candidate; unchanged settings issue no ALTER.
sequences_settings_description: Existing sequences have Settings, Source and Information tabs. New sequences open only the creation form. Saving settings and restarting numbering are deliberately separate actions.
sequences_settings_heading: Settings tab — name, range and numbering policy
sequences_source_1_2: Read Oracle DBMS_METADATA DDL or PostgreSQL’s reconstructed CREATE SEQUENCE from metadata.
sequences_source_1_3: PostgreSQL retains the existing data type/settings and includes OWNED BY when appropriate. This text is not generated from unapplied setting inputs.
sequences_source_2_2: Use Refresh to fetch source or Retry after a source error.
sequences_source_2_3: Refreshes the source snapshot without consuming numbers or discarding settings edits. A source-read error disables its copy action until a successful load.
sequences_source_3_2: Use the copy icon after source loading succeeds.
sequences_source_3_3: Copies DDL without executing it. The source editor is read-only and has no compile/save or Git-history control on this tab.
sequences_source_4_2: Review the source note and ensure any owning table/column exists before using copied SQL.
sequences_source_4_3: CREATE does not restore the exact next number. PostgreSQL IDENTITY ownership is noted, not recreated by a normal OWNED BY clause; recreate that association through the table definition.
sequences_source_description: Available for existing sequences. This is a read-only creation reference, not an editable migration or an exact backup of the current numbering position.
sequences_source_heading: Source tab — creation DDL and copy
sequences_step_1: Open the sequence, wait for metadata and inspect limits, cache/options, data type and usage. Treat the observed reference as metadata, not a guaranteed next number.
sequences_step_2: Save intended setting changes separately from a restart. Review conflicts, reload DB values or keep local edits for a new checked save.
sequences_step_3: Use Restart only when moving subsequent numbering deliberately; confirm target/value and inspect ownership/dependencies. Use Source only as creation reference, not exact numbering-state recovery.
sequences_summary: Review limits, caching and explicit restarts.
sequences_workflow_body: Open an existing sequence, wait for metadata, change Increment from 1 to 10 and Save only the settings. This applies the step change without resetting the numbering position. Inspect current settings and dependencies afterward. If you truly need numbering to restart from 1000, separately enter 1000 as the restart candidate and review the named confirmation; do not infer that a shown metadata value is the next application ID.
sequences_workflow_heading: Example: change the step without restarting
settings_actions_description: Edits remain a draft until Save succeeds. Empty or out-of-range numeric values must be corrected before saving.
settings_ai_description: Set the assistant’s send shortcut and request limits. Capacity is measured in MiB (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes), not tokens. New limits apply to the next request.
settings_ai_idle_effect: Limits the wait for response headers or the next response data. Continuous streaming can continue within the separate total timeout.
settings_ai_response_effect: Caps the received response body, including JSON, streaming chunks and error responses. Exceeding it stops reception and prevents adopting an incomplete answer. Raising it allows larger responses; it does not increase the model’s token limit.
settings_ai_send_effect: Changes keyboard submission in the AI assistant. Cmd is used on macOS and Ctrl on Windows. The Send button remains available.
settings_ai_send_value: Enter sends / Shift+Enter inserts a line break; or Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends / Enter inserts a line break
settings_ai_total_effect: Limits total request time, including compatibility retries. Reaching the limit stops the request without an automatic retry after that limit.
settings_apply_body: Click Save after editing. Language and style update the local app presentation; SQL timeout is captured when connecting, so reconnect to use a new value. Some screens load formatting settings when opened, so reopen the screen if its display has not changed. New AI limits apply to the next request, and file limits apply when files are opened. Settings do not change database privileges or commit or roll back a transaction.
settings_cancel_effect: Closes the dialog without saving the current edits. Previously saved settings remain in use.
settings_defaults_effect: Replaces the draft values with the dialog’s defaults; Save is still required. It does not erase database data or SQL history. The draft language is kept as English or Japanese, date defaults follow it, and the reset timezone is +09:00 (the first-launch timezone is detected from the OS).
settings_er_file_effect: Caps loading saved custom ER diagram files and their Git revisions. Increasing it allows larger diagrams while format/content checks remain in place.
settings_files_description: Limits apply when opening supported files. Raising a capacity limit does not disable file-type or regular-file checks. Values are in MiB.
settings_general_description: Language, date handling, query limits and SQL history. The timezone selector uses fixed UTC offsets, not city-based daylight-saving rules.
settings_history_enabled_effect: Off stops saving new history while retaining existing history. Recognized credential-changing SQL is excluded even when history is on.
settings_history_limit_effect: Controls the maximum number of entries retained when new SQL history is saved. Older entries beyond the limit are removed during that save; changing this value alone is not a command to erase all history.
settings_input_date_effect: Sets the expected date format for supported date fields, filters and data editing. Match typed dates to the selected format; it is separate from the display format.
settings_input_date_value: YYYY/MM/DD, YYYY-MM-DD, MM/DD/YYYY, DD/MM/YYYY or DD-MMM-YY; each with or without HH:mm:ss
settings_intro: Settings control the local application experience. Language and theme change presentation; timeouts, file limits and AI limits constrain operations. Configure these deliberately for your workload.
settings_language_effect: Changes the desktop app’s menus, labels and messages. It does not change SQL identifiers or the website language.
settings_max_tabs_effect: Limits how many workspace tabs can be opened. At the limit, opening another tab is refused with a message; existing tabs are not automatically closed.
settings_note: The website language selector changes the manual language only. It does not change the language stored in your desktop application settings.
settings_number_effect: Changes the grouping separator for aggregated values in cross-tab results. It does not change stored numeric values or every numeric display in the app.
settings_oracle_client_effect: Specifies the client libraries used for Oracle Thick mode, including OS authentication. It does not install Oracle Client. Reconnect after changing it; if Thick mode is already initialized, restart the app to change the loaded library.
settings_oracle_client_value: 64-bit Instant Client / Oracle Home folder; can be blank
settings_oracle_description: Oracle-specific client configuration. This setting is not used for PostgreSQL connections.
settings_output_date_effect: Changes supported date/time displays in results and related screens. For example, 2026/10/30 09:00:00 can be shown as 2026-10-30 09:00:00. It does not change the database column type.
settings_output_date_value: YYYY/MM/DD HH:mm:ss; YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss; MM/DD/YYYY HH:mm:ss; DD/MM/YYYY HH:mm:ss; DD-MMM-YY HH:mm:ss
settings_provider_body: This dialog’s AI tab controls the send shortcut and limits. Enable AI support and configure the endpoint URL, model and API key in the separate AI Settings dialog from the AI menu. Changing a response limit does not connect a provider or send a request.
settings_provider_title: AI provider connection settings are separate
settings_query_timeout_effect: Sets the main connection’s query timeout for the next connection, so reconnect after saving. Oracle times database calls; PostgreSQL configures query/statement timeouts. It is not a single time budget for an entire multi-statement script. Background and management operations may have separate limits.
settings_save_effect: Writes the settings and updates the app after saving succeeds. If saving fails, correct the problem and retry; the change is not treated as successfully applied.
settings_sql_file_effect: Rejects SQL files larger than the limit when opening them in the SQL window. Partial content is not loaded. This limits file opening, not the number of SQL result rows.
settings_step_1: Open Settings → Settings… from the app menu, then choose the General, View, Oracle, AI or Files tab. You can also open the dialog before connecting.
settings_step_2: Use the tables above to choose valid values and review their effects. Save changes; reopen affected screens or reconnect where indicated.
settings_step_3: Use the separate AI Settings dialog for provider credentials. The AI tab here sets send shortcuts and limits only. Keep secrets out of shared screenshots.
settings_summary: Tune appearance, limits, history and AI behavior.
settings_theme_effect: Changes the app palette, including panels, editors and result grids. All three styles have the same database features; compare their screenshots in the App styles guide.
settings_timezone_effect: Chooses the UTC offset used for supported date/time handling. Oracle also sets the session time zone when connecting; reconnect after changing it. This does not rewrite PostgreSQL server timezone settings.
settings_view_description: Choose the app appearance and the date/number formats used by the relevant screens. These settings do not rewrite values stored in the database.
site_ai_boundary_body: The AI provider does not receive a database connection or a tool for executing SQL. MonaBase sends the context you approve; applying source, executing SQL and inserting data remain application actions you review and initiate. Selected source and trace values are still sent to your provider.
site_ai_boundary_title: Your context in. A proposal out.
site_ai_coding_body: Create or revise procedures, functions, package bodies and triggers with selected object definitions as context. Review the source diff before adopting a proposal.
site_ai_data_body: Describe the sample data you need for the selected table. Use AI assistance alongside generation rules and a preview; insertion remains a separate action under your control.
site_ai_debug_body: Send recorded execution order, source lines and variable values to AI. Ask it to reconstruct a pseudo step-through, explain a branch or find where a value first diverged from expectations.
site_ai_feature_body: Five integrated assistants help with stored code, trace debugging, SQL creation, SQL tuning and data generation. Choose an OpenAI-compatible provider, preview the context, and review proposals before applying them.
site_ai_provider_body: Configure a model and an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint, including compatible hosted services or local providers. You are not tied to one AI vendor; available features and context limits depend on the chosen service and model.
site_ai_sql_body: Describe the query you need from the SQL window or query builder. Add the relevant tables and views, then inspect the proposed SQL before running it.
site_ai_tuning_body: Bring SQL, execution-plan information and related definitions into a tuning request. Review suggested changes and compare actual plans and results before adopting them.
site_ai_workflows_intro: AI is integrated with the screen you are working in, not just a generic chat box. MonaBase prepares relevant source, metadata, plans or recorded traces for a focused request that you control.
site_ai_workflows_title:
An assistant for each stage
of database development.

site_readonly_body: Use a read-only connection for inspection. MonaBase checks allowed SQL and uses database read-only transactions, while blocking updates, stored execution and trace execution in this mode.
site_review_body: Connection colors identify the target. Preview AI requests and source diffs, review import/generation data, and confirm consequential operations before applying them.
site_safety_intro: Explicit transaction controls, read-only connections and deliberate review steps help reduce accidental changes in production workflows. Combine these protections with a database account that has only the privileges your task needs.
