types_source_1_2: Edit the displayed definition with SQL highlighting, line numbers and schema completion.
types_source_1_3: Changes an editing draft; the Source asterisk means it differs from the loaded/saved baseline. It is not an automatic DB save.
types_source_2_2: Keep the opened schema/name and use the supported CREATE TYPE form for that database.
types_source_2_3: Rejects target changes and unsupported/multiple statements before applying a definition. PostgreSQL also refuses type-kind changes; use a separately reviewed SQL workflow for other migrations.
types_source_3_2: Oracle: click Compile. PostgreSQL: click Save (Execute) and inspect the generated change dialog when changes exist.
types_source_3_3: Oracle executes the TYPE definition and checks diagnostics. PostgreSQL plans supported ALTER changes instead of issuing CREATE against the existing type.
types_source_4_2: Use Retry after a definition/metadata read fails; wait for a successful load before applying or deleting.
types_source_4_3: Keeps apply/delete disabled while the source is unready and preserves an existing edited draft during reload. A failed read is not an empty type.
types_source_5_2: Click Delete, review the exact target and dependent objects, then confirm deliberately.
types_source_5_3: Issues DROP TYPE; PostgreSQL explicitly uses RESTRICT. It does not silently add FORCE/CASCADE or remove and recreate dependents; Git cleanup is a separate operation.
types_source_6_2: Read diagnostics in the lower console, click a line-numbered message to jump to source, or use the trash icon to clear messages.
types_source_6_3: Helps locate problems. Clearing messages does not roll back applied DDL; this type window does not execute methods to populate RETURN/OUT results.
types_source_7_2: Wait for active reads/execution; close a PostgreSQL change preview before returning to source editing.
types_source_7_3: Locks conflicting controls while busy and prevents editing the reviewed source while its change dialog is open.
types_source_description: Both database versions have Source, Version control and Information tabs. This window maintains the opened type; the CREATE text is a definition to review, not a generic new-type creation form or a routine execution window.
types_source_heading: Source tab — edit the opened type
types_step_1: Open the type and inspect Information for kind, attributes/labels, any Oracle body and direct dependencies. Preserve the current source before changes.
types_step_2: Edit within the supported scope. On Oracle compile the TYPE declaration; on PostgreSQL save the desired definition and review its generated ALTER plan.
types_step_3: Inspect DB status/diagnostics, any completed/pending changes and separate Git outcomes. After a partial failure, recompute the remaining difference instead of blindly rerunning old SQL.
types_summary: Inspect and maintain database-specific type definitions.
types_version_1_2: Inspect/copy current text and check whether Source has an asterisk.
types_version_1_3: May include unapplied edits. Copying CREATE text does not create or replace the DB type.
types_version_2_2: Use the source refresh icon after an external change or when validating saved state.
types_version_2_3: Reloads the saved baseline while preserving an existing edited draft. Refresh is not a command to discard all local edits.
types_version_3_2: Record the reviewed definition with a useful message; configured AI can help summarize changes.
types_version_3_3: Records a local source version. Successful apply also attempts Git recording; a Git error is reported separately from an already successful DB save.
types_version_4_2: Select history, compare two revisions or review changes across schema objects.
types_version_4_3: Shows definition differences without applying them. Include users of the type when reviewing impact; a source diff does not analyze every application consumer.
types_version_5_2: Select an intended revision and inspect its SQL before running anything.
types_version_5_3: Does not automatically revert ENUM additions or dependent data. A historical CREATE definition can require a separate migration and must respect the editor’s supported-change limits.
types_version_6_2: Verify repository/remote settings and use Push or refresh Git state as needed.
types_version_6_3: Transfers source history or reads repository state. It does not apply the type to another database.
types_version_description: Configure local Git before recording. The shared version-control view receives the type editor text; DB apply, local source recording and remote Push are separate operations.
types_version_heading: Version control tab — type source history
views_data_1_2: Set conditions and click Execute. Opening the Data tab also performs an initial search after column information is available.
views_data_1_3: Runs a matching-row count and fetches the first result page. It queries the view, not each underlying table separately.
views_data_2_1: Find a column / active conditions only
views_data_2_2: Enter part of a column name or enable the active-only checkbox.
views_data_2_3: Filters the condition editor only. Conditions in hidden columns remain; a status message reports hidden active columns.
views_data_3_2: Choose String, Number or Date; PostgreSQL also provides Time only. Read the date/time field example before entering a value.
views_data_3_3: Changes how the search value is validated and converted. Excluded column types are unavailable for filtering or sorting; the view column type itself is unchanged.
views_data_4_2: Choose equality, inequality, less-than-or-equal, greater-than-or-equal or LIKE. Leave a value empty to omit that column filter.
views_data_4_3: Different column filters use AND. LIKE means literal substring matching; % and _ in the input are treated as characters rather than user wildcards.
views_data_5_2: Enter 1, 2, 1 DESC or ASC/DESC in the sort fields.
views_data_5_3: Smaller priority numbers sort first. ASC is ascending and DESC descending. Without a distinguishing sort, equal-valued rows can appear in a different order across pages or queries.
views_data_6_2: Click a condition-enabled column header in normal view.
views_data_6_3: Immediately searches page one, toggles ascending/descending for that column and clears other sort fields. This action is disabled in transposed view.
views_data_7_2: Clear the entered conditions, then click Execute to confirm the new result.
views_data_7_3: Resets condition/sort inputs. Clearing alone does not replace displayed rows.
views_data_8_2: Choose 50, 100 or 500 rows and move with the controls below the grid.
views_data_8_3: Fetches the requested page with the current input conditions. Changing page size returns to page one. It does not load the whole view into the grid.
views_data_9_1: Changing conditions before paging or export
views_data_9_2: After editing or clearing a condition, click Execute before moving pages or exporting.
views_data_9_3: Unlike the table window, view paging and normal export use current inputs. An old result can stay on screen until the next query, so execute first to align it with the intended filters.
views_data_description: The Data tab reads the view results. It has no record insert/update/delete or import controls, even if the database supports updates through that view. Definition editing is a separate operation on the Edit tab.
views_data_heading: Data tab — filters, sorting and paging
views_db_behavior_body: Oracle VIEW DDL follows implicit-commit rules, and a FORCE definition can produce an invalid view whose errors need inspection. PostgreSQL CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW restricts changes to existing output column names, order and types; a rejected replacement is not a reason to automatically drop the view. Both the editor and Git history need to be checked against the actual DB result. This guide describes ordinary views; materialized-view refresh is covered by its own guide.
views_edit_1_2: Edit the loaded definition, keeping its schema-qualified view name. Use line numbers and schema/object completion to navigate.
views_edit_1_3: Changes a local editing draft only; the DB is unchanged until Save/Compile is executed. The SQL dialect and completion match Oracle or PostgreSQL.
views_edit_2_2: Check whether the Edit tab has an asterisk before leaving or recording source.
views_edit_2_3: Indicates a difference between the editing text and the last saved/loaded source; it is not a Git push status or an automatic file save.
views_edit_3_2: Use Compile (Save) on Oracle or Save (Compile) on PostgreSQL after reviewing the definition.
views_edit_3_3: Executes the VIEW definition on the main DB connection. Successful DDL invalidates cached data/metadata and updates the sidebar; it is not merely a syntax preview.
views_edit_4_2: Keep exactly one VIEW declaration with the opened schema and name. Use the SQL window for other SQL or migrations.
views_edit_4_3: Rejects a different target, unqualified view name, multiple statements or another object type before sending the definition for execution.
views_edit_5_2: Use Retry in the source error message and wait for a successful load.
views_edit_5_3: Save is disabled until a valid source load succeeds. A refresh preserves an existing edited draft rather than silently replacing it with fetched text.
views_edit_6_2: Read the console and editor error markers after a failure. Oracle also checks VIEW errors after DDL; PostgreSQL can report a statement position.
views_edit_6_3: Helps locate invalid definitions without treating a failed compile as a clean save. On Oracle, a FORCE definition can leave an invalid object in the DB; inspect Information as well.
views_edit_7_2: After a successful compile, read any Git failure message separately.
views_edit_7_3: The app attempts to record the updated source in Git. A Git failure does not undo the successful DB change; fix Git and record again instead of assuming DB save failed.
views_edit_8_2: Click Delete, review the confirmation and required privileges, then proceed deliberately.
views_edit_8_3: Issues DROP VIEW, not DELETE against its base-table rows. Dependencies may prevent deletion; the action also attempts Git source removal and closes the tab on completion.
views_edit_9_2: The console opens when messages arrive. Drag its boundary, close it with × or clear its messages with the trash icon.
views_edit_9_3: Changes the log presentation only. Hiding or clearing messages does not undo a view definition or repair an error.
views_edit_description: This editor changes the database VIEW definition, not a SQL file. Only one CREATE [OR REPLACE] VIEW statement explicitly naming the opened schema and view is accepted.
views_edit_heading: Edit tab — save the view definition
views_information_1_2: Use the outlined refresh button, or Retry after a metadata error.
views_information_1_3: Reloads status, columns and direct dependencies. It does not compile a view or fetch result rows; a read failure is shown as an error, not an empty dependency list.
views_information_2_2: Read the status line above the column list.
views_information_2_3: Oracle shows the catalog status such as VALID/INVALID. PostgreSQL marks an existing ordinary view as VALID; this is not a performance assessment or a guarantee that every user can query it.
views_information_3_2: Inspect column names, data types and NULL information.
views_information_3_3: Shows the output shape exposed by the view. NULL metadata reflects the catalog and is not a guarantee that an expression can never return NULL.
views_information_4_2: Read the schema, name and type of the objects used by the view.
views_information_4_3: Identifies upstream dependencies such as base tables and other views so you can investigate a missing object or changed definition.
views_information_5_2: Read the objects that depend on this view.
views_information_5_3: Helps assess downstream impact. PostgreSQL lists catalog-linked dependent views/materialized views through rewrite rules; Oracle uses ALL_DEPENDENCIES.
views_information_6_2: Treat the lists as direct dependencies visible through the current database catalogs and privileges.
views_information_6_3: Does not enumerate every recursive dependency, application query, dynamic SQL or inaccessible object. An empty list does not prove that a view has no external users.
views_information_description: Information is a read-only catalog view, separate from the editable definition and returned records. Read the dependency direction before changing or deleting the view.
views_information_heading: Information tab — columns, status and dependencies
views_intro: The view window has four tabs: Data, Edit, Version control and Information. Data reads the view results; Edit saves the database definition; Version control manages source history; Information shows catalog status, columns and direct dependencies. The tables below distinguish these operations and their effects.
views_oracle: Oracle compilation diagnostics and object status help identify an invalid view.
views_postgresql: PostgreSQL replacement rules can restrict changes to existing output columns. Review the actual result rather than assuming a replacement succeeded.
views_results_1_2: Use the swap-axes icon below the result grid; click again to return.
views_results_1_3: Shows the currently loaded page with fields as rows. Normal paging is hidden during transposed display; it does not fetch all view rows.
views_results_2_2: Open the download icon and choose Clipboard, CSV or Excel; choose a destination path for a file.
views_results_2_3: Creates tab-separated clipboard text or a file. Normal export fetches all rows matching current filters, not only the visible page; transposed export uses the loaded transformed result.
views_results_3_2: Choose whether to include headers, select UTF-8 or Shift-JIS for CSV, and toggle protection for formula-like text.
views_results_3_3: Controls output text and spreadsheet interpretation. Protection may add a leading apostrophe; review the raw-value trade-off before disabling it.
views_results_4_2: Read fetch/prepare/save status and use Stop while export data is being fetched.
views_results_4_3: Stops further export fetching without altering database data. Normal export issues additional queries, so large or expensive views may take time.
views_results_5_2: Read SQL, result messages and errors in Execution log; use its trash icon to clear logs, or drag the divider to resize the condition area.
views_results_5_3: Changes the visible log or screen layout. A read/count failure is an error, not proof of zero rows; clearing the log does not resolve the failure.
views_results_description: The result grid is read-only. These tools change presentation or export data; they do not modify records in the underlying tables.
views_results_heading: Data tab — result tools and export
views_step_1: Open a view and inspect Information for its columns, status, references and dependents. Preserve the existing definition in Git before changing it.
views_step_2: Edit the single schema-qualified VIEW definition and save/compile deliberately. Resolve source-load or compile errors and distinguish DB success from a Git-recording failure.
views_step_3: Verify returned rows and refreshed Information after the change. Execute edited filters before paging/export, then review source history and downstream objects.
views_summary: Review a view definition, dependencies and returned rows.
views_version_1_2: Read or copy the source currently held in the editor.
views_version_1_3: Copies definition text without executing it. Check the Edit asterisk if you need the compiled DB definition rather than a draft.
views_version_2_2: Use the refresh icon to read the DB definition again.
views_version_2_3: Refreshes the loaded-source baseline. Existing edits are preserved, so an asterisk may remain; refresh is not a discard-draft command.
views_version_3_2: Record the reviewed source and optionally enter a commit message; a configured AI can assist with the change summary.
views_version_3_3: Creates a local source-history commit. It does not compile the draft into the DB or automatically publish it to GitHub; AI assistance sends a request only when used.
views_version_4_2: Select a commit in the history and read the source comparison.
views_version_4_3: Shows saved source and differences from the current text; selecting a revision does not replace the DB view.
views_version_5_2: Choose two revisions for comparison, or open the schema-change review.
views_version_5_3: Expands review beyond one current-versus-history comparison or one object. These are review tools, not automatic DB migrations.
views_version_6_2: Select the intended history entry and open its recovery SQL.
views_version_6_3: Opens SQL for inspection and deliberate execution. It does not immediately restore the view; review dependent objects, replacement rules and privileges first.
views_version_7_2: Reload history when it changes, and use the shared Push operation after checking the configured repository and remote.
views_version_7_3: Refresh reads Git state; Push sends source commits to the remote. Neither operation deploys the view definition to the DB.
views_version_description: Set up the local Git repository from the app menu before using recording/history operations. The version-control view receives the editor text, so a draft is not necessarily the definition currently installed in the DB.
views_version_heading: Version control tab — source history and comparison
views_workflow_body: First inspect Information for columns and dependencies, then preserve the current source in Git. In Edit, change the SELECT while keeping the opened schema-qualified VIEW name, and run Save/Compile. Read the console and status, distinguishing DB errors from Git-recording errors. Return to Data, set the intended filters and run Execute before paging or export. Finally compare the recorded source and verify dependent views as needed.

workspace_intro: The sidebar groups objects by schema and category. The main area keeps object editors and tools in tabs. Connection identity stays visible so you can confirm the target before running SQL or changing definitions.
workspace_note: A category or command can be absent because it is database-specific or your account lacks privileges. A failed refresh is not proof that the database has no objects.
workspace_step_1: Select a schema, expand a category and search for an object. Load additional entries when the category has more results.
workspace_step_2: Open an object to inspect its data, definition or information. Use the context menu to see the operations available for that object.
workspace_step_3: Use open-tab search to locate a tab; choose it with the arrow keys and Enter. Recheck the connection color and schema before a change.
workspace_summary: Find objects and move between working tabs.
